description: Adversarial Wave 0 (ROADMAP Tasks 239, 573) over the 314 keys that detect_english_drift.php reports NEW or CHANGED since the 2026-08-09 sync and that do not already carry a $ec_lang_syn (wave0_keyset.php --new-and-changed). Three agents took ~105 keys each and read every one against its real call site, asking not 'is this good English?' but 'list every plausible reading'. Result: 136 findings on 314 keys (30 high, 102 medium, 4 low); 178 keys read and dismissed. Every entry is open: this pass proposes, it does not write. $ec_lang_syn is off-limits to AI by standing rule, so anything routed there is a proposal awaiting written permission. | SPRINT CLOSE 2026-09-02: 26 languages delivered, 223 missing keys and 97 stale ones each. The translators' own suggestion box produced 40 further findings across 16 keys, and three of them were defects in English that no reviewer had caught: lpn_run_menu_tip told the user to press a Run button that had been renamed Calculate in this same sprint, and lpn_field_demand_pattern_tip named the default pattern control by a label it does not have. A third report, on lpn_quality_needs_run, was already fixed on the tree and is recorded as dismissed. Two more were defects in our own guidance rather than in the English: the glossary's emitter renderings were the irrigation dripper, refused independently by ru, bn and bg, and the three fire flow terms shipped with empty translations maps so every language coined its own.

entries.complaint: medium: Rendered both as a link's visible text and as the title= of a one-character "X" link that collapses a RESULTS ROW (lib/Calculators.lib.php:490) and, on the calculator pages, a row of related-calculator links. "Line" has no antecedent in the string, and in a hydraulics suite "line" is also a pipeline. The control is a toggle, so it also shows.
readings: hide this row of the table (intended)
hide this pipe/line on a drawing
hide this line of text
entries.resolution: Dismissed. Every one of the 26 shipped translations already renders the row / line-of-text sense (fr 'ligne', ru 'строку', zh '行', id 'baris'); not one took the pipeline reading. The English works as measured, and 'Hide this row' would buy 26 retranslations of a three-word string to fix a defect nobody has committed.

entries.complaint: medium: The subject is elided: 'May not be valid' never says WHAT may not be valid. Attached to the EGL and HGL input labels on three pages (Manning-Pipe-Head-Loss, Darcy-Weisbach, Hazen-Williams). Most target languages must supply a subject and a gender for it, so each translator picks one, and they will not pick the same one. 'See notes' also names no notes: these three pages have no notes section the tip can point at.
readings: this computed EGL/HGL value may not be valid (intended)
this whole calculation method may not be valid
this input may not be valid
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'This result may not be valid where the pipe rises above the hydraulic grade line.' The elided subject is supplied and 'See notes.' is dropped, because none of the three pages carrying this tip has a notes section it could point at.

entries.complaint: medium: Ends in a bare adjective with no noun: 'economical' agrees with nothing. Gendered languages must invent an antecedent (the loss? the pipe? the design?) and will not agree with each other. Its two siblings (mhp_hl_warn_tip, mhp_hl_bad_tip) are full sentences with an imperative, so the set is not parallel. Also carries an em dash in visitor-facing English.
readings: the PIPE/design is economical (intended)
the head loss is economical
this is the economical case
entries.resolution: English fixed, parallel with its two siblings and one em dash lighter. Now: 'Head loss is under 10% of gross head. This pipe size is economical.'

entries.complaint: medium: First sentence says the equations are 'based on steep channel slope and unit discharge', then Equation 1 is said to apply for gentle slopes (S0 < 0.10). An English reader stumbles; a translator must decide whether 'steep' qualifies the domain or is part of the variable name, and if they read it as the domain the sentence contradicts the next one.
readings: based on channel slope and unit discharge, over a range that includes steep slopes (intended)
based on the slope of steep channels only, which then contradicts the gentle-slope clause
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'based on steep channel slope and unit discharge' is now 'from channel slope and unit discharge'; the two equations' stated ranges carry the domain, which is where the contradiction was coming from.

entries.complaint: high: A bare toolbar mode label. In graph theory and in every network textbook a VERTEX IS A NODE, and this page's own nodes are junctions/reservoirs/tanks. A translator with only this word will reasonably render it with their language's word for graph node, and the button will then claim to add network nodes when it adds bend points on a pipe. The tip (lpn_tool_vertices_tip) disambiguates but is a separate key and may be translated by a different pass.
readings: the intermediate shape points of a pipe polyline (intended, and EPANET's own word)
the nodes of the network graph
corner points of a polygon
entries.resolution: Glossary. The term 'vertex' already existed and was already wired to lpn; its avoid array now carries the graph-theory sense in so many words ('a vertex IS a node' is the reading to refuse) and the bend-fitting sense, and its context names the toolbar mode. English 'Vertices' stands: it is EPANET's own word.

entries.complaint: high: Uses 'bend' four times for a polyline vertex. In hydraulics a BEND is a fitting with a minor loss coefficient, and this page models exactly that (EngCalcs.lpnLinkK, minor loss k). A translator rendering 'bend' with their word for the fitting produces a tip claiming the tool adds and removes fittings, which is a false statement about the hydraulics.
readings: a geometric bend point in the drawn route of the pipe (intended)
a bend fitting, an elbow, which adds a minor loss
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'Add and remove the vertices that shape a pipe on the map. Click a pipe to add a vertex, click a vertex to remove it, and drag a vertex to move it. A vertex changes only the drawn route, not the hydraulics.' Four uses of 'bend' are gone; in hydraulics a bend is a fitting with a minor loss coefficient, which this page models, so the old tip claimed the tool added and removed fittings.

entries.complaint: high: A dangling preposition on a read-only property row whose object lives in the value cell beside it (js/looped-network.js:25770 prints lb.anchorNode || lb.anchorLink). The string alone never says what the Text is attached to, and this is precisely the shape four translators voted down on lpn_pump_curve_source in sprint 241 ('Curve from' -> 'Curve source').
readings: a label naming what this Text is anchored to (intended)
a fragment awaiting a noun the translator cannot see
a past participle describing the Text: 'attached to ...' as a state
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'Attached to' is now 'Attached asset': a noun phrase with no dangling preposition, matching how sprint 241 resolved lpn_pump_curve_source. 'Anchor' was rejected because an anchor block is a real water-works object.

entries.complaint: medium: 'placed in a real location' can mean either that it now sits somewhere on the real Earth (it is put at Novato, CA, which has nothing to do with Net3) or that it has been put back where the real Net3 system is. The second reading is a false claim about EPA's network, and it is the reading a reader who knows Net3 will take first.
readings: put down at an actual place on the globe, chosen for the demonstration (intended)
put back at the true real-world location of the Net3 system
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'The same network as EPANET Net3, put down at an arbitrary place on the globe: its coordinates are latitude and longitude, and a street map is drawn behind it.' 'an arbitrary place on the globe' closes the false reading that Net3 has been put back where the real system is.

entries.complaint: high: The heading of the units warning, over a body that lists which fields the unit governs. This page's absolute rule is that changing a unit REINTERPRETS the number already typed and never converts it. 'decides what your inputs mean' is true under that rule but reads equally well as 'decides how your inputs are converted', which is the opposite behaviour. A translator who takes the conversion reading writes a heading that is false about the product.
readings: choosing this unit changes what the numbers already in the project mean (intended)
choosing this unit changes how the numbers are converted
choosing this unit is decided by what you have entered
entries.resolution: Dismissed, and the proposed English would have been FALSE. This dialog offers BOTH answers: lpn_units_nondestructive_desc ('leaves every input as it is and reinterprets it in the new unit') and lpn_units_destructive_desc ('rewrites every input with a mathematical conversion'). A title saying 'it does not convert them' contradicts the second option in the same box. The title is Tom's own wording (2026-08-18, Task 425), and the two option descriptions resolve the conversion reading inside the same dialog and the same payload.

entries.complaint: medium: Two soft spots in one sentence. 'no standard number to compare it against' can be a regulatory limit or a typical value; 'read it as a measurement and judge it yourself' is a phrase with no obvious technical anchor, and 'measurement' is odd for a computed quantity, which will push a translator toward the reading that it was measured in the field.
readings: there is no regulatory or code limit for water age, so judge the number in context (intended)
there is no typical value published, so you have nothing to compare with
treat the figure as a field measurement
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'How long the water reaching this point has been in the system. There is no regulatory limit to compare it against, so judge the number against your own system.'

entries.complaint: medium: Carries three unglossed terms in one sentence: 'source trace', 'source trace share' and 'trace node'. CLAUDE.md deliberately splits the ANALYSIS (Source trace) from the NUMBER (Source share), and this tip is the only place that ties them, yet the compound 'the source trace share' is a fourth form appearing nowhere else. glossary.json has no entry for source trace or trace node, so nothing tells a translator these are EPANET's own named analysis and named node.
readings: the share reported by the Source trace analysis (intended)
the share of the source that is being traced
a share belonging to a thing called a source-trace
entries.resolution: English fixed and two glossary terms added. Tip now: 'How much of the water reaching this point came from the trace node. This is what the Source trace analysis reports.' New wired-to-lpn terms 'source trace' (EPANET's analysis) and 'trace node' (the node it follows), each carrying the avoid list for the two other senses of 'source' on this page. The fourth form 'the source trace share' is gone.

entries.complaint: medium: A top-level nav label. On this page 'map' names two different things: the drawing surface itself (used that way in lpn_tool_add_reservoir_tip, 'Click the map') and the raster street/satellite basemap behind it. The menu holds basemap and readout choices, so the intended sense is the second, but a translator seeing one word picks whichever their language distinguishes.
readings: the street/satellite basemap and what is drawn over it (intended)
the drawing surface, the canvas the network is drawn on
the verb, to map
entries.resolution: Dismissed. The menu governs the basemap AND what is drawn over it, so both readings land on the same menu and neither produces a wrong control. One word is right for a nav bar. PROPOSAL LEFT UNWRITTEN (AI may not touch $ec_lang_syn): $ec_lang_syn['lpn_menu_map']='Map, Basemap, Background map, Street map | layout: nav item'.

entries.complaint: medium: 'Import xy to lat/lon' has no expressed object, so the two coordinate systems are the only nouns and either can be the thing imported. It also does not say a FILE is involved, though the row opens a file picker. The JS fallback says 'Import XY to lat/lon' with different capitalisation from the shipped string, which will show translators two spellings of the same token.
readings: open a file whose coordinates are xy and place it on the lat/lon map (intended)
import lat/lon data into the current xy project
import a conversion, an xy-to-lat/lon transform
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'Open an xy file on the map…' It names the object (a file), says a file is involved, and drops the bare xy/lat-lon preposition pair. The JS fallback at js/looped-network.js was carrying a third spelling ('Import XY to lat/lon…') and now matches. lpn_new_coords_tip's citation of the row was updated in the same pass.

entries.complaint: high: Two problems. (1) 'in a new tab' means one of THIS PAGE'S project tabs (openAsGeoFile lands the text with newTab true), not a browser tab; a translator has no way to know and the browser-tab reading is a false statement about what happens. (2) 'one button says so and the network jumps straight to where it belongs' is not recoverable: the button is lpn_georef_asdeg_btn, 'These are already lat/lon', and 'says so' means the user presses it to declare it, not that the interface announces it.
readings: a new project tab inside this page (intended)
a new browser tab or window
there is a button you press to say the coordinates are already lat/lon (intended)
a button appears telling you that the coordinates are lat/lon
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'Opens a project file or an EPANET file in a new project tab on this page, on the street map. You place the drawing on the world by hand: pan and zoom to the site, then size and turn it to fit. If the x and y in the file already are a longitude and a latitude, press the These are already lat/lon button and the network jumps straight to where it belongs. Every number you typed stays as it is.' 'a new project tab on this page' kills the browser-tab reading, and the button is named under the new convention instead of 'one button says so'.

entries.complaint: high: Ends 'then press Put the model here'. That phrase is the LABEL OF A BUTTON, lpn_georef_drop, and nothing in the string marks it as a quotation. A translator will render it as ordinary prose, in whatever wording fits the sentence, and it will then not match the button they see on screen. Same defect in lpn_georef_step1_hint (same phrase) and lpn_georef_asdegrees. Additionally 'Step 2 is the fine one' uses a third adjective for a step the label calls 'precise'.
readings: press the button labelled Put the model here (intended, quoted control name)
put the model here, as an instruction phrased freely
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'Placing the model takes two steps. Step 1 is the quick one: the model holds still and you move the map behind it, until your site is under the model at about the right size. There is no rotation yet. Step 2 is the precise one: you drag, resize and rotate the model itself. Your project is on a map of the whole world to start with, so find your location first, then press the Put the model here button.' The button is named as 'the Put the model here button' per the convention recorded in dev/language-strings.md, 'the fine one' becomes 'the precise one' to match lpn_georef_step2, and 'turning' becomes 'rotation' throughout. lpn_georef_step1_hint and lpn_georef_asdegrees carry the same button in the same shape.

entries.complaint: high: 'press Keep this placement' quotes the label of lpn_georef_finish with no marking. Same class as lpn_georef_intro: translated as free prose it will not match the button.
readings: press the button labelled Keep this placement (intended)
keep this placement, as free advice
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'The model now sits on the two points you gave. Check it, then press the Keep this placement button.'

entries.complaint: high: 'Use Background image > Move to line it up' is a MENU PATH, two control labels and a separator, embedded in prose. Nothing marks it, so a translator renders it freely and it stops naming anything on screen. 'line it up' is also idiomatic: 'align' is the operation.
readings: open the Background image menu and choose Move (intended)
move the background image, as a free instruction
draw a line along it
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'The background image was moved and resized with the model, but it could not be rotated. Use Map, Background image, Move to align it.' The menu path is comma-separated (the shipped majority: 19 comma paths against 3 arrow ones), the Map menu is named so the path is complete, and 'line it up' becomes 'align it'.

entries.complaint: high: Carries a quoted setting label twice ('Recalculate automatically') and a menu path ('in Settings, under Calculation, Hydraulics'), none of it marked as a control name, plus a control name in the question ('a Run button'). Three separate cross-key matches a translator cannot see. 'To restore it' also reads as restoring defaults rather than bringing the button back.
readings: turn off the setting named Recalculate automatically, found under Settings > Calculation > Hydraulics (intended)
turn off automatic recalculation by some means, wording free
restore defaults
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'Recalculate this network now. Looking for the Run button? It is hidden while the Recalculate automatically setting is on. To bring the button back, turn Recalculate automatically off in Settings, Calculation, Hydraulics.' The curly quotes are gone; the setting and the button are each named with their widget word, and the menu path is comma-separated. 'To restore it' is now 'To bring the button back', so the restore-defaults reading is closed.

entries.complaint: medium: 'Or type the scale and the turn below' uses 'the turn' as a NOUN for the rotation angle. It is not a term any engineer or GIS user would recognise, and js/looped-network.js records that Tom chose ROTATED over 'turned' for lpn_georef_backdrop_unrotated, so the page already says both. The two controls it points at are lpn_georef_scale ('Ground distance per drawing unit') and lpn_georef_rotation ('Turn anticlockwise (degrees)'), so 'the scale' does not match its control's label either.
readings: the rotation angle you type in the box below (intended)
the act of turning
a turn as in a bend in the route
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'The model is on the ground now, so it moves with the map. Drag the model to move it, drag a corner to resize it, drag the round handle above the model to rotate it. Or type the ground distance and the rotation angle below.' 'the turn' as a noun is gone; 'the scale' becomes 'the ground distance' so it matches its control (lpn_georef_scale, 'Ground distance per drawing unit').

entries.complaint: medium: 'The place, the size and the turn all follow from those two.' Three nouns, none of them the conventional term: position, scale and rotation. 'the turn' repeats the invention flagged on lpn_georef_adjust, and 'the place' is being used for position. 'those two' also has to reach back two sentences to 'points'.
readings: the position, the scale and the rotation are all computed from the two points (intended)
the location, the size of the site, and a turn in the route
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'Place the model exactly, when you already know where two points on your drawing really are. Click one of them, type its latitude and longitude, then do the same for a second point. The position, the scale and the rotation all follow from those two points. Press this button again to stop picking.' Position, scale and rotation are named conventionally and 'those two points' no longer reaches back two sentences.

entries.complaint: medium: A window.confirm, so the user is committing an irreversible change of project kind while reading it. 'You can still drag single assets afterwards' can mean 'one at a time' or 'individual, unattached ones'. The second reading suggests a limitation that does not exist and could stop a user confirming.
readings: you can still drag assets one at a time (intended)
you can still drag assets that are on their own, not connected ones
you can drag a single asset only once
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'drag single assets' is now 'drag assets one at a time', which is the only reading left. Now: 'Place the model here permanently? You can still drag assets one at a time afterwards, but the drawing stops being an xy project. To get xy back, close this project without saving.'

entries.complaint: medium: 'static for this project' has two readings that lead to opposite user behaviour, and the word 'Manual' is a control value quoted without marking (same class as the georef button names). 'sets the boundaries based on the current state of the system' also leaves open whether it recomputes them as the network changes, which is exactly what 'static' is trying to deny.
readings: the boundaries do not update on their own as results change (intended)
the boundaries are stored with this project rather than with the browser
the boundaries cannot be changed
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'The boundaries below are fixed once set; they do not follow the results as they change. Choosing a data classification method above sets the boundaries from the current state of the system. If you change any value by hand, the method above becomes Manual.' 'static for this project' is replaced by what it was trying to say, and 'becomes Manual' names the option the method select shows.

entries.complaint: high: 'so the number of colors is fixed while it is chosen' reads most naturally as 'during the act of choosing', which would be a false statement: the count is fixed for as long as the method is SELECTED, not while the user is picking. 'it' also has two candidate antecedents in the sentence, the method and the standard.
readings: the number of colors stays fixed for as long as this method is selected (intended)
the number of colors is temporarily fixed while you are making the choice
while the design standard is chosen
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'This method takes its boundaries from a design standard, so the number of colors is fixed while this method is selected.' 'while it is chosen' becomes 'while this method is selected', which removes both the during-the-act reading and the second antecedent.

entries.complaint: medium: A verbless fragment ('These parts shown as a table you can sort'), which several target languages cannot render without inventing a main verb, and each will invent a different one. 'These parts' also has no antecedent inside the string: it is the tip on every one of the six tab buttons. 'Results are read-only' can mean the result COLUMNS cannot be edited or that the whole table is read-only, which is false, since the tip itself is on an editable table (lpn_tables_menu_tip says 'you can sort it and edit it there').
readings: this tab shows the parts of this kind as a sortable table (intended)
these parts are shown as a table somewhere else
the whole table is read-only
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'This tab shows the assets of this kind as a table you can sort and edit. Result columns cannot be edited.' The fragment gains a main verb, 'This tab' supplies the antecedent, and 'Result columns' says which part is read-only, which is what the table actually does.

entries.complaint: low: 'none of these' points at a tab the string cannot see; used at four call sites, all of them a per-kind table or library list. Translators must choose a gender and number for 'these' with no antecedent.
readings: this network has no parts of this kind yet (intended)
this network has none of the things just listed
entries.resolution: Dismissed. The six tab call sites and the four library ones share no true noun: junctions, pipes, patterns, curves and controls are not all 'assets'. Every call site prints this line directly under a heading that names the kind, which is the reason the code comment gives for one message serving all of them, and it holds. Severity was low.

entries.complaint: medium: A toggle whose two labels are not parallel: on it says 'Reduce map clutter', off it says 'Show map readouts' (lpn_clean_map_off). One names a goal, the other names the object, so a translator sees no pair. Worse, 'clutter' does not say WHAT is removed, and on a network map the obvious clutter is the labels and annotation, which this control does not touch: it removes the mode line and the coordinate readout. A user who takes the label at face value presses it expecting the labels to thin out.
readings: hide the on-screen readouts so a screenshot is clean (intended)
thin out the network labels and annotation on the drawing
simplify the basemap
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'Reduce map clutter' is now 'Hide map readouts', parallel with its own off state 'Show map readouts' and true about what the control removes. The screenshot purpose stays in the tip.

entries.complaint: medium: 'the mode line' is an internal name for the status strip and appears in no other visitor-facing string, so it names nothing a user or translator can identify. 'off the picture' and 'only the map' use two words for the same surface in one sentence, which reads as though the picture and the map are different things. Also carries an em dash.
readings: remove the status strip and the coordinate readout from the drawing surface (intended)
remove a line drawn on the map
the picture and the map are two separate layers
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'Take the status strip and the coordinate readout off the map, so a screenshot shows only the drawing. Your drawing is not touched, and this choice is not stored; reloading the page brings the readouts back.' 'the mode line' becomes 'the status strip', the picture/map split is resolved onto one surface, and the em dash goes with the rewrite.

entries.complaint: medium: The value is 'Water' under a key named lpn_menu_project, deliberately (Task 523). A translator reading the key name and the value together has to decide which one is the label, and 'Water' alone as a nav item can be the substance, an adjective, or a shortened 'Water network'. Its tip resolves it but is a separate key.
readings: the menu holding everything about water network modelling (intended)
the project menu
water as a substance or a quality parameter
entries.resolution: Dismissed. 'Water' is the deliberate value under this key (Task 523) and one word is right for a nav bar; the key-name-versus-value tension is a translator reading the key name, which is not the label. PROPOSAL LEFT UNWRITTEN (AI may not touch $ec_lang_syn): $ec_lang_syn['lpn_menu_project']='Water, Water network, Water system, Network | layout: nav item'.

entries.complaint: medium: 'find every part that meets a test' uses 'test' where the interface means a condition or criterion; 'test' in a hydraulics tool also reads as a field or pressure test. The string also uses 'part', while 44 other shipped lpn strings say 'asset' and 7 say 'element' for the same thing, so the suite ships three words for one concept and each translator resolves it separately.
readings: find every asset matching a condition you build (intended)
find every asset that passes a test, as in a hydraulic or pressure test
find every part, meaning a component of an asset
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'Find an asset by its ID, or find every asset matching a condition, and change them all at once.' 'test' becomes 'condition' and 'part' becomes 'asset'. On the asset/part/element split: ASSET WINS by incumbency, measured at 44 shipped strings against 7 for 'element', and every string this pass touched now says asset.

entries.complaint: medium: A template, '{n} highest', used both as a pull-down row (where the code prints the letter n literally) and as text the query parser must match back. 'highest' names no quantity, and in many languages the count must follow the superlative, so the translator has to know {n} may move and must survive. Nothing in the string says {n} is a placeholder rather than a literal.
readings: the n assets with the highest value of the chosen property (intended)
the highest of n
n, printed as a literal letter
entries.resolution: Intent. The English stands: '{n} highest' pairs with '{n} lowest' and a longer form would not fit a pull-down row. What was missing was the instruction about the placeholder, and it now reaches every translator in every payload: meta.placeholder_notes in dev/scripts/generate_translation_payloads.php says a braced word is replaced at runtime, must be kept exactly, must never be translated, and MAY be moved to wherever the language needs it.

entries.complaint: high: A property name in the Find pull-down, whose operators are all connectivity tests (no links at node, no path to a source). In water utility English a CONNECTION is a service connection, the tap serving a customer, and that is the first reading a utility engineer or their translator will take. Translated that way the property claims to search service connections and returns nodes.
readings: connectivity, whether the node is joined to the rest of the network (intended)
a service connection, a customer tap
a joint or fitting between two pipes
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'Connection' is now 'Connectivity'. It names the four tests underneath it and removes the service-connection reading, which is what a utility engineer reads first.

entries.complaint: medium: 'open' here is EPANET's LINK STATUS, the opposite of closed, and it must not be read as 'available', 'unobstructed' or 'exposed'. Nothing in the string or in glossary.json says so, and the whole conn family depends on it (lpn_find_op_conn_noopen, _noopensource, lpn_find_conn_noopen, _noopensource). A translator taking the everyday reading produces a filter that appears to search for unobstructed paths.
readings: no link at this node whose status is OPEN (intended)
no link at this node that is unobstructed or free
no link at this node that is exposed or above ground
entries.resolution: Glossary. New term 'open (link status)', wired to the lpn prefix, giving EPANET's OPEN/CLOSED sense and an avoid array against 'unobstructed', 'available' and 'exposed'. The whole conn family inherits it; the English is unchanged because it is EPANET's own word.

entries.complaint: medium: 'a source' means a fixed-head node, a reservoir or tank, as lpn_find_conn_no_fixed states. But this same page uses 'source' for the water-quality trace node (lpn_result_source_share) and for a value's origin (lpn_replace_source, 'New value from'). Three senses of one word in one interface, and this string carries no clue which one it means.
readings: a reservoir or tank, a fixed-head supply node (intended)
the trace node of a source trace analysis
the origin of a value
entries.resolution: Glossary, English unchanged. ALL FOUR connectivity operator wordings are Tom's own (2026-08-26, the local pair reworded by him 2026-08-29; recorded in dev/lpn-spike/find-harness.js), so 'a source' stands. The three-senses-of-source problem is answered by the new wired term 'source trace', whose avoid array names both other senses explicitly: the value-origin sense ('New value source') and 'a source meaning a reservoir or tank, which is the sense the Find connectivity operators use'.

entries.complaint: medium: Quotes two operator names, 'no links' and 'no open links', that match NO label on screen: the pull-down rows are 'no links at node' and 'no open links at node' (lpn_find_op_conn_unlinked, _noopen). A translator will translate these two short forms freshly and produce a third wording, and the user is being told to look for text that does not exist.
readings: only the two operators named no links at node and no open links at node can be searched (intended)
two differently named options the user must hunt for
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'This network has no reservoir or tank, so there is no source to reach. Only no links at node and no open links at node can be searched.' The two quoted short forms are replaced by the operators' actual full labels, so the user is told to look for text that exists.

entries.complaint: medium: Three unanchored pronouns in two clauses: 'it rewrites itself', 'type in it', 'the controls follow'. 'The controls follow' can mean the controls update to match what you typed or that the controls appear below the query box.
readings: change the controls and the query text is rewritten; type in the query text and the controls update to match (intended)
the controls are laid out below the query box
the query rewrites the controls
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'The same search, written as one line. Changing the controls rewrites this line, and typing in this line updates the controls.' All three pronouns are replaced by their referents.

entries.complaint: medium: 'Expandable with AND, OR, and ()' is a hint under a text box, so 'expandable' reads first as a claim about the BOX (it can be made bigger) rather than about the query. It is also the only string in the batch with no verb the reader can act on.
readings: you can combine conditions using AND, OR and parentheses (intended)
the input box can be expanded
the results can be expanded
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'Expandable with AND, OR, and ()' is now 'Combine conditions with AND, OR and ()': a verb the reader can act on, and no claim about the box.

entries.complaint: medium: AND and OR are both the visible pull-down labels AND words the query parser matches (findJoinDefs returns ['and', label, 'AND']; findAlts accepts the English token as well as the translation). So a translator faces a word that looks like syntax and cannot tell whether translating it will break a query. The safe-looking choice, leaving it English, is also legitimate, so the 26 languages will split.
readings: a translatable label for the joining word (intended, and the parser also accepts the translation)
a literal keyword of a query syntax that must stay in English
entries.resolution: Glossary. New term 'query keyword (AND, OR)', wired to lpn, which MAKES the decision instead of leaving it to 26 guesses: translate them, the parser accepts both the English token and the translation, and leaving them English is not safer. The English is unchanged.

entries.complaint: medium: 'These controls cannot write the query below' means the controls cannot EXPRESS what the query says. 'Write' reads as a permission or a capability of the widget rather than a statement about expressive range, and 'so they are hidden' then reads as a fault rather than a design choice.
readings: the controls cannot express this query, so they are hidden (intended)
the controls are not allowed to modify the query text
the controls failed to write the query
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'cannot write the query below' is now 'cannot express the query below', which is the statement about expressive range that was meant.

entries.complaint: medium: 'This query cannot be read' reads as a legibility or permissions problem rather than a parse failure, and 'there is nothing to change' can be taken as 'nothing matched' rather than 'the replace cannot run'. Between them a user is told a true thing in a way that names the wrong cause.
readings: the query cannot be parsed, so no replacement can run (intended)
nothing in the network matched the query
the query text could not be loaded
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'This query cannot be understood, so nothing can be changed. Fix it above first.' 'cannot be read' becomes 'cannot be understood' (a parse failure, not a legibility one) and 'there is nothing to change' becomes 'nothing can be changed'.

entries.complaint: medium: 'Not something to search' is an unusual construction that reads as a judgement ('this is not worth searching') rather than as 'there is no such thing to search in'. The subject, {w}, arrives after the colon, so the translator must build a sentence whose subject is a runtime token.
readings: there is no searchable kind of asset called {w} (intended)
{w} is not worth searching
{w} cannot be searched for
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'There is nothing called {w} to search. Try one of: {list}' The subject is inside the sentence and the judgement reading is gone.

entries.complaint: medium: Ends with the literal example 'Junction.ID'. Both halves are also visible pull-down labels, and the parser accepts either the translation or the English token, so a translator cannot tell whether the example is syntax to preserve verbatim or an example to localise. Both choices work at runtime, which means nothing will ever reveal the split.
readings: a literal example of query syntax, keep it as it is
an example using the interface's own words, so translate it to match this language's Junction and ID labels
entries.resolution: Glossary. Covered by the same new 'query keyword (AND, OR)' term as finding 36, which names the Junction.ID example explicitly: translate Junction and ID to match this language's own labels for them, and the dot stays a dot. English unchanged.

entries.complaint: medium: 'bracket' names '[' in US usage and '(' in British usage; the character shown is a parenthesis. A translator working from the word rather than the glyph will name the wrong character, and the message's whole job is to tell the user which character to type. Same in lpn_find_q_err_open.
readings: parenthesis, the ( character shown in the message (intended)
square bracket
any grouping character
entries.resolution: English fixed in both siblings: 'This parenthesis ( was opened and never closed.' and 'This parenthesis ) closes nothing.'. 'Bracket' is '[' in US usage and '(' in British; the message's whole job is to name the character shown.

entries.complaint: high: 'New value from' is a dangling preposition on a select label whose object lives in the select beside it, the same defect four translators independently voted down on lpn_pump_curve_source in sprint 241. The JS fallback at looped-network.js:9604 says only 'From', so the two forms of the label disagree as well. The options are 'The number above' and 'Mapbox DEM', so the label must read as naming a source of values.
readings: a label naming where the new value comes from (intended)
a fragment awaiting a noun the translator cannot see
an instruction, take a new value from ...
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'New value from' is now 'New value source', the same resolution four translators demanded of lpn_pump_curve_source in sprint 241. The JS fallback, which said only 'From', now matches.

entries.complaint: high: The whole message is deictic. It reports that elevations were requested from the Mapbox DEM for {n} nodes and that the answers are still on the wire, but the string names neither the elevations, nor the nodes, nor the service. 'Asked for {n}' with a bare number is not a sentence a translator can safely build, and 'The answer is on its way' will be read as a single answer arriving, or as an apology, rather than as pending network requests.
readings: elevations were requested for {n} nodes and the results are still arriving (intended)
{n} things were requested and one answer is coming
a request was made and a reply is expected soon, in general
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'Elevations requested for {n} nodes. The results are on their way.' The elevations, the nodes and the plurality of the pending requests are all named.

entries.complaint: medium: The saved-profile menu heading says 'paths', while glossary.json carries the concept as 'profile (long section)' and the key itself is lpn_profile_*. A translator given 'Saved paths' with no glossary link will render the route sense, and the pane in question draws a long section. Five sibling keys in this batch repeat 'path' (lpn_profile_new, _rename, _delete, _prompt_name, _delete_confirm, _none_saved, _missing).
readings: a saved profile, the long section along a chosen line of nodes (intended)
a saved route or itinerary
a file path
entries.resolution: Glossary. New term 'path (profile route)', wired to lpn, naming what is actually saved (the ordered list of nodes a profile is drawn along) and refusing the file-path reading, the itinerary reading, and confusion with the Find connectivity 'link path'. The English family keeps 'path' because the saved object IS the route, not the drawing; 'profile (long section)' already covers the drawing and is already wired.

entries.complaint: medium: '{name} names nodes that are not in this project' puts a runtime token in subject position followed by the verb 'names', which reads first as the plural noun. An English reader stumbles ('{name} names' looks like a noun phrase), and a translator who takes it that way produces a fragment.
readings: the saved path called {name} refers to nodes that are missing (intended)
{name} is a list of names of nodes
the names of {name} are not in this project
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'The saved path {name} uses nodes that are not in this project: {ids}' The runtime token is out of subject position, so '{name} names' can no longer read as a noun phrase.

entries.complaint: medium: One of two radio labels for a project's COORDINATE SYSTEM, beside 'lat/lon'. 'xy grid' reads equally as a drawing grid or snap grid, which is a different feature a CAD-literate user expects to find. Its sibling names a coordinate system with no such second reading, so the pair is not balanced.
readings: a plain xy coordinate system, any coordinates that are not lat/lon (intended)
a grid drawn on the canvas, a snap grid
grid coordinates in the surveying sense
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'xy grid' is now 'xy coordinates', parallel with 'lat/lon' and matching what lpn_new_coords_tip already says. The mode name itself is still 'xy' (lpn_xymap), so mode_name_check.php is unaffected; verified.

entries.complaint: low: "An xy project is a model on any coordinates other than lat/lon" uses "on" for the coordinate system a model is expressed in, which no other string in the suite does, and "any" reads as permissive rather than as a definition. A translator has to decide whether the sentence is defining a term or granting freedom. The menu path it cites was verified and is correct (lpn_file_import_geo = 'Import xy to lat/lon').
readings: a DEFINITION: an xy project is one whose coordinates are not geographic (intended)
a PERMISSION: an xy project may use whatever coordinates you like
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'An xy project uses coordinates that are not latitude and longitude. A lat/lon project has geographic coordinates, so a street map or satellite picture can be drawn behind it and node elevations can be read from the terrain. An xy project can be converted to lat/lon with File, Open an xy file on the map.' 'a model on any coordinates other than lat/lon' becomes a definition, and the cited menu row moved with finding 12 and is comma-separated.

entries.complaint: medium: A placeholder holding a real US town. Nothing in the string, the key name or the call site tells a translator whether this is content to localize or a fixed example to carry through verbatim. The two answers produce visibly different products, and 26 agents will not choose the same one. This is the whole finding: the English is fine, the INSTRUCTION is missing.
readings: a sample of the KIND of thing to type, to be replaced with a town the reader will recognise
a fixed proper noun to leave in English, like an eponym
entries.resolution: Dismissed. It is a search-box placeholder: a translator who localizes the town and one who carries Petaluma through both ship a working hint, so the two answers differ visibly and cost nothing. Not worth a permanent instruction. PROPOSAL LEFT UNWRITTEN (AI may not touch $ec_lang_syn): $ec_lang_syn['lpn_new_place_hint']='Paris, France; Nairobi, Kenya; Bogota, Colombia | a placeholder example of a town and its region; use a place a reader of this language will recognise, spelled as that language spells it'.

entries.complaint: medium: Two problems in one sentence. "what it holds that this page keeps without using" stacks two relative clauses on one head noun, and "what changed on the way in" is an English idiom for 'what was altered during import' that reads spatially when calqued. A translator cannot tell whether the report lists things the FILE contains or things the PAGE changed, which is the one distinction the sentence exists to draw.
readings: a list of file contents kept but unused, plus a list of import-time changes (intended)
a list of things the page keeps changing as you work
'on the way in' read as a physical route rather than as 'during import'
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'This page does not use everything EPANET does, but nothing in your file is thrown away. Below is what your file holds that this page keeps without using, and what was changed when the file was read in:' The two stacked relative clauses are separated and 'on the way in' is spelled out as 'when the file was read in'.

entries.complaint: medium: "nothing is holding pressure or flow there any more" turns on the verb 'hold'. In water distribution 'holding pressure' can mean maintaining it (intended, what a PRV/PSV does) or retaining/containing it (what a closed valve or a vessel does). A translator picking the second sense writes a sentence saying the network no longer contains pressure, which is false.
readings: nothing MAINTAINS the pressure or the flow at that point any more (intended)
nothing CONTAINS or holds back pressure or flow there any more
nothing is holding the pressure or flow steady at a stored value
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'nothing is holding pressure or flow there any more' is now 'nothing controls pressure or flow there any more', which is what a PRV/PSV does and cannot be read as containment.

entries.complaint: medium: "where more of it enters" has two candidate antecedents for 'it' one clause apart: 'the water quality' (the grammatical subject of the sentence) and 'what is in the water' (the substance, the intended one). Languages with gendered pronouns must commit, and half of them will commit wrongly. Verified against the call site: this covers EPANET's QUALITY, SOURCES, REACTIONS and MIXING sections, so the referent really is the constituent.
readings: where more of the SUBSTANCE enters the network (intended: EPANET [SOURCES])
where more WATER enters the network
where more of the water-quality description appears in the file
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'where more of it enters' is now 'where more of that substance enters', naming EPANET's [SOURCES] referent so no gendered language has to guess.

entries.complaint: medium: "a part that this page does not read at all" - 'part' is the wrong noun in a water context, where a part is a fitting or a component of an asset. The thing meant is an EPANET file SECTION, which is what the key name says and what the code case ('other-sections') says. A translator reading the string alone will render the component sense.
readings: a SECTION of the EPANET file (intended)
a PART or fitting belonging to the network
a portion of the network model
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'a part that this page does not read at all' is now 'a section', which is what the key name and the code case both say and removes the fitting reading.

entries.complaint: medium: "every junction here receives the demand the file states whatever pressure results" is a garden path: 'states whatever pressure results' parses as a complete clause, so the sentence first reads as the file stating a pressure. There is no punctuation to block it. The correct reading is concessive ('no matter what pressure results') and the two readings say opposite things about what the file contains.
readings: the junction gets the file's demand REGARDLESS of the resulting pressure (intended)
the file states whatever pressure results, and the junction gets that demand
the demand the file states is whatever pressure comes out
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'This file asks for a pressure-driven analysis (PDA), in which a junction receives less than its demand when the pressure there is low. This page solves demand-driven, so every junction here receives the demand the file states, no matter what pressure results. The line is kept and is written back if you save an EPANET file.' The garden path is blocked with a comma and 'no matter what pressure results'.

entries.complaint: medium: "This file was imported from EPANET. Some information here was not imported." reads as a contradiction, and 'here' has two referents: this page, or this file. A translator who takes 'here' as the file writes a sentence saying part of the file was left behind, which contradicts lpn_inp_report_lead's promise that nothing is thrown away.
readings: some of what the file holds is kept but not used by this page (intended)
some information in the file was dropped during import
some information shown on this page did not come from the file
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'This project was read in from an EPANET file. Some of what that file holds is kept but is not used on this page.' The apparent contradiction is gone and 'here' is replaced by the two things it could have meant.

entries.complaint: high: "Water quality is not modeled" is FALSE as written, and the batch contains its own contradiction: lpn_inp_drop_quality says 'This page works out water age and source trace', and water age and source trace ARE water quality analyses in EPANET's own vocabulary (they are options of the QUALITY setting). A translator has no way to see that the sentence means 'water quality CHEMISTRY is not modeled', so 26 languages ship a flat false claim under the heading 'Not modeled'. Second, weaker ambiguity in the same string: 'the EPANET solver, which this page turns on by itself when your network holds one' - 'one' should attach to the valves, but the nearest noun is 'solver'.
readings: no water quality analysis of any kind is done (false, and the likeliest reading)
the water quality CHEMISTRY is not modeled, though age and source trace are (intended)
'when your network holds one' = holds one such valve (intended) vs holds one solver
entries.resolution: English fixed, and this was a FALSE claim under a 'Not modeled' heading. Now: 'Water quality chemistry is not modeled; water age and source trace are. Valves: a throttle valve works in either solver, and the valves that set their own position (PRV, PSV, FCV) are solved with the EPANET solver, which this page turns on by itself when your network holds one of those valves.'

entries.complaint: medium: "Find picks out every asset that meets a test" - 'a test' has no established sense here. In engineering copy a test is a physical or acceptance test; the thing meant is a search condition the user builds in the Find dialog. 'Find' is also unmarked as a command name, so a translator may render it as the ordinary verb and lose the tie to the menu row.
readings: every asset matching a search condition you set (intended)
every asset that passes an engineering check or acceptance test
'Find' as the ordinary verb rather than as the name of the command
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'every asset that meets a test' is now 'every asset that matches a condition you set', and Find is left capitalised as the command it names.

entries.complaint: medium: "To get new boundaries, choose a method again or type your own." - the nearest noun to 'your own' is 'a method', but what the user types is BOUNDARIES. The sentence therefore invites a reading in which the user writes their own classification method, which the page does not offer.
readings: type your own band boundaries (intended)
type your own classification method
type your own colors
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'choose a method again or type your own' is now '...or type your own boundaries', so the nearest-noun reading (writing your own classification method) is closed.

entries.complaint: medium: The diagnostic counts 'iterations' while every setting that controls the same quantity counts 'trials' (lpn_settings_trials 'Maximum trials', lpn_settings_unbalanced_trials, lpn_settings_accuracy_tip 'from one trial to the next'). EPANET's own name is MAXTRIALS. Two English words for one concept become two unrelated words in 26 languages, and the user cannot connect the failure message to the box that would fix it.
readings: iterations = the solver trials the Maximum trials box limits (intended)
iterations = something other than trials, since the settings use a different word
entries.resolution: Dismissed, and the proposed change would have undone a ruling made the same day. EPANET names the INPUT EN_Option.Trials and the REPORTED COUNT EN_AnalysisStatistic.Iterations; this string prints the reported count. Tom asked on 2026-09-02 whether the two words were standing in for one thing and the toolkit's own enums answered that they are not (dev/lpn-spike/convergence-honesty-harness.js records it). 'iterations' is correct here and 'trials' on the settings is correct there.

entries.complaint: medium: "at a relative error of {error}, against an accuracy of {accuracy}" - 'against' is doing comparison work that many languages express with a different preposition, and 'an accuracy of' reads as a measured property of the answer rather than as the name of the setting the user typed. Same iterations/trials split as its sibling.
readings: compared with the Accuracy SETTING, which it failed to reach (intended)
with an achieved accuracy of {accuracy}
measured against an accuracy target of unspecified origin
entries.resolution: English fixed, in the half that was real. Now: 'It stopped after {iterations} iterations at a relative error of {error}, which did not reach the Accuracy setting of {accuracy}.' 'against an accuracy of' named no owner; it now names the Accuracy setting. The iterations/trials half is DISMISSED for the reason on the sibling finding: EPANET reports iterations and limits trials, and they are two quantities.

entries.complaint: medium: "The bends in every pipe are shown as grips." 'Grip' as a draggable square handle is CAD vocabulary (AutoCAD), not general English and not EPANET's. Outside that context it is a hold, a handgrip, or friction. It appears nowhere else in this batch, so a translator has only the sentence.
readings: a small square handle you can drag (intended, CAD sense)
a hold or handle in the physical sense
traction or friction
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'Mode: Vertices. The vertices of every pipe are shown as small square handles. Click a pipe to add a vertex, click a handle to remove it, or drag a handle to move it. Nothing else on the map is changed in this mode.' 'Grip' is AutoCAD vocabulary and appears in no other visitor-facing string; the mode line now says vertex where the object is a vertex and handle where the object is the thing you drag.

entries.complaint: high: "Nothing is picked." The page's mode is called Select (lpn_tool_select = 'Select', and its own synonym entry lists 'pick' only as an alternate for the TRANSLATOR, not as the shipped word). Substituting 'picked' for 'selected' in the one message that tells the user what to do next is the exact pattern Tom struck four times (rest pressure, pulled down, settle, the usual value): a plainer synonym replacing the conventional term. A translator will render 'picked' with a word unrelated to whatever they used for Select mode, and the instruction stops pointing at the tool.
readings: nothing is SELECTED, in the sense of Select mode (intended)
nothing has been chosen from a list
nothing has been picked up / collected
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'Nothing is picked.' is now 'Nothing is selected.', pointing at Select mode (lpn_tool_select). This was the struck pattern exactly: a plainer synonym displacing the shipped term.

entries.complaint: high: "Click the map to place a text label." This collides head-on with the one vocabulary split the project has deliberately declared (Task 482): our Label is EPANET's annotation, and our Text is the free-standing object this mode places. Calling the Text object 'a text label' hands 26 translators the other object's name. Every other string in this batch keeps them apart (lpn_settings_color_thematic_tip says 'Text you placed yourself').
readings: a Text object, the free-standing one this mode places (intended)
a Label, the map annotation that prints an asset's properties
a generic textual caption belonging to neither object
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'Mode: Add Text. Click the map to place a Text. Click near a node to attach the Text to that node. Switch to Select mode to change or move assets and labels.' 'a text label' handed 26 translators the OTHER object's name; Task 482's split is that our Label is EPANET's annotation and our Text is this free-standing object.

entries.complaint: medium: "so you can pick out the two ends without reading the numbers" - on a pipe network page 'ends' is a live geometric term (the two ends of a pipe, an end node). The intended sense is the two extremes of a value range. Secondly, 'the highest value of each kind' leaves 'kind' open between kind of asset and kind of value; the code marks extrema per property, so it is the second.
readings: the two extremes of the value range, highest and lowest (intended)
the two ends of a pipe
'each kind' = each asset type vs each labelled property (the second is intended)
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'Draws a line above the highest value of each labelled property on the map (an overline), and a line below the lowest value of that property (an underline), so you can pick out the highest and the lowest without reading the numbers.' 'each kind' becomes 'each labelled property' (which is what the code marks) and 'the two ends' becomes 'the highest and the lowest', off the pipe-end reading.

entries.complaint: medium: "the one whose remaining value is worth showing least" is a superlative that inverts under a wrong parse: 'worth showing least' (least worth showing, intended) against 'worth showing the least [value]'. The wrong parse says the page hides the label with the SMALLEST number, which is not what the code does for pressure (it hides the one nearest the middle of the range). Note the string also carries an em dash; if it is edited for this, drop the dash per the standing advisory. 'Given up' is deliberate and glossary-anchored ('drop (a label)'), so it is NOT a finding.
readings: the label least worth showing is hidden (intended)
the label carrying the smallest number is hidden
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'The order in which properties are given up when two node labels would overlap. The property numbered 1 is given up first, on both labels. When one property is left and the two still overlap, a whole label is hidden: whichever label’s remaining value is the least worth showing, which means the lowest demand, the pressure nearest the middle of the range, or the elevation or head closest to the neighbouring nodes.' The superlative can no longer invert, and the em dash went with the rewrite.

entries.complaint: medium: "Apply these values to all assets" - 'these values' points at nothing the string can see. The button sits under the New-assets defaults block (lpn_settings_defaults_note), so 'these' means the new-asset defaults; but a user with the property popup open reads it as the values on the asset in front of them. Its own confirm text (lpn_push_confirm) has to spell out 'the values now set for new assets', which is evidence the button does not.
readings: the values set for NEW assets, applied to every existing one (intended)
the values currently shown in the property popup
the values in whatever settings section is open
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'Apply these values to all assets' is now 'Apply these new-asset values to every existing asset', so the button says what its own confirm text had to spell out for it.

entries.complaint: medium: Two findings in one string. (a) It says 'element' where 40 other lpn_ values say 'asset' - measured: only this key and lpn_control_dangling_note still say element. One concept, two English words, so 26 languages get two. (b) 'Ringed:' opens the sentence as a bare past participle with no subject, which several languages will read as an imperative or as a heading.
readings: 'element' = the same thing the rest of the page calls an asset (intended)
'element' = something narrower than an asset, e.g. a component of one
'Ringed:' as a label for what the amber ring means (intended) vs as an instruction to ring something
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'The amber ring means this asset holds a value that belongs to the scenario {name} alone.' 'element' becomes 'asset' (the 44-to-7 incumbent) and the bare participle 'Ringed:' becomes a sentence with a subject.

entries.complaint: medium: "Switch to Base to see the drawing without them." 'Base' here is the name of the base scenario and has its own key (lpn_scenario_base = 'Base', with a gloss pointer and an avoid list against the chemical, foundation and military senses). Embedded as a bare capitalised word in another string, it will be translated a second time, independently, and the two renderings will not match, so the instruction names a control that is not on the screen.
readings: the scenario named Base, i.e. lpn_scenario_base (intended)
an ordinary English word meaning the underlying or original state
the chemical / foundation senses the glossary already warns about
entries.resolution: English fixed AND the code changed. The string now reads 'Each of those values is marked on the map with an amber ring. Switch to {base} to see the drawing without them.' and js/looped-network.js substitutes pc.lpn_scenario_base into {base}, the pattern lpn_push_base_only already uses. The base scenario's name is now spelled in exactly one key.

entries.complaint: medium: "Clear this box" - the control is a checkbox (verified: input.type='checkbox' at js/looped-network.js:25886), and 'clear a box' is idiomatic for BOTH unchecking a checkbox and emptying a text box. Every other field in this popup is a text box. A translator who chooses the erase sense writes an instruction that cannot be carried out, on the control that decides whether an asset is in the solve.
readings: untick the checkbox (intended)
erase the contents of the box
reset the box to its default
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'Clear this box' is now 'Uncheck this box'. Verified against the call site: the control is input.type='checkbox' and every other field in that popup is a text box, so the erase reading was an instruction that could not be carried out.

entries.complaint: high: "The power in the sprinkler and leak law, flow = coefficient x pressure to this power." Two defects. (a) 'Power' is used twice for EXPONENT on a page that models pumps, where power is energy per unit time and is the reading a hydraulic engineer reaches for first; several languages have no word covering both senses, so the translator must choose and half will choose watts. (b) 'the sprinkler and leak law' names nothing. EPANET calls this the emitter, and the setting itself is EMITTER EXPONENT; a translator searching for the named law finds no literature. This is the same class as the struck 'rest pressure': an invented plain name displacing a term of art.
readings: exponent (intended)
power in the energy sense, which is what a pump page primes the reader for
'the sprinkler and leak law' as a citable named law vs as a description of the emitter equation
entries.resolution: English fixed and the glossary extended. Tip now: 'The exponent in EPANET's emitter equation for sprinklers and leaks: flow = coefficient x pressure raised to this exponent. It only changes the answer where a node has an emitter, which for now means a network read from an EPANET file.' 'Power' becomes 'exponent' twice, and 'the sprinkler and leak law' becomes EPANET's emitter equation. The existing 'emitter' term gained the EPANET sense and an avoid array against the watts reading; it is now wired to lpn as well as ip.

entries.complaint: medium: A two-word button whose first word is a noun, a verb and an adjective in English. 'Sample' as 'take one reading of' is the intended verb; 'a sample' and 'sample (= example)' are both live and both produce a button that promises something else. Its sibling button is 'Use DEM', which is unambiguously imperative, so the pair does not disambiguate itself. DEM is also an untranslated acronym that the tip expands only as 'Mapbox DEM'.
readings: read one elevation from the DEM at this node (intended)
an example DEM, or a demonstration
a specimen or extract of the DEM data
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'Sample DEM' is now 'Read DEM', an unambiguous imperative parallel with its sibling 'Use DEM'. The noun and example senses of 'sample' are both gone.

entries.complaint: medium: "shows it below for review before changing the current entry" says that a change to the entry is coming. It is not: Sample only displays, and it is the separate Use DEM button that writes the Elevation box (lpn_elev_dem_use_tip). A translator rendering the temporal reading writes a tip promising an action the button does not take, which is exactly the behaviour Task 542 exists to have removed.
readings: shows the value so you can look at it; nothing is changed (intended)
shows the value, then changes the entry
shows the value so you can review it before it changes the entry for you
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'Reads the elevation of the DEM at this node and shows it below. Nothing in the Elevation box is changed. The horizontal DEM resolution is about 30 m for most of the Earth, and finer where better data exists.' The tip no longer promises a change the button does not make; that is the Task 542 defect class.

entries.complaint: medium: "The DEM gave no height for this node." 'Height' and 'elevation' are different quantities in hydraulics (height above local ground vs elevation above a datum), and the box this message sits under is called Elevation. Every other string in the elevation group says elevation; this one does not, so it is the one that will be translated with a different word.
readings: no elevation value came back for this node (intended)
no height above ground came back
the DEM returned a value of zero height
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'gave no height' is now 'has no elevation', matching the box it sits under and every other string in the elevation group.

entries.complaint: medium: "Elevation from" is a dangling preposition on a select label: the object of 'from' lives in the <select> beside it and is invisible to the translator. This is the identical shape to lpn_pump_curve_source, which all four anchor languages independently flagged in sprint 241 and which was rewritten to a noun phrase for this reason. Repeating it invites the same four reports.
readings: a label naming the SOURCE of a new node's elevation (intended)
a sentence fragment awaiting a noun the translator cannot see
'from' read as the start of a range (elevation from X to Y)
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'Elevation from' is now 'Elevation source', the sprint-241 resolution applied to the identical shape. CLAUDE.md and dev/geographic-projects.md both name this control and were updated in the same pass.

entries.complaint: medium: "The number above" is a select option whose meaning depends entirely on spatial layout the translator cannot see, and 'above' is relative to whatever the reader takes as the reference: the Elevation default box in the same Settings block (intended), the select itself, or the previous option in the list. Its sibling option ('Mapbox DEM') names its source outright, so the pair is not parallel.
readings: the elevation value typed in the box above this control (intended, per the key name)
the number in the row directly above in the list
a number appearing higher up the Settings panel generally
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'The number above' is now 'The elevation typed above': parallel with its sibling 'Mapbox DEM' in naming its source, and it survives a layout change.

entries.complaint: medium: Two ambiguities. (a) 'measured as the flow still changing from one trial to the next' uses a bare participle where a noun is meant (the amount by which flow still changes). (b) 'Left empty, this page tries far harder than EPANET does on its own' - 'tries harder' on a page whose adjacent settings are Maximum TRIALS and Extra TRIALS reads as running more trials, when it means using a tighter accuracy. That wrong reading contradicts lpn_settings_trials.
readings: uses a stricter default accuracy than EPANET's own (intended)
runs more trials than EPANET would
makes a greater effort in some unspecified way
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'How close the solver has to get before it stops, measured as the amount by which the flows are still changing from one trial to the next. A smaller number is more exact and takes longer. Both solvers read this one box, and each measures that change against a different total: the built-in solver against the sum of the demands, EPANET against the sum of the link flows. Left empty, this page uses a stricter accuracy than EPANET's own default.' The bare participle becomes 'the amount by which the flows are still changing', and 'tries far harder' becomes 'uses a stricter accuracy', which cannot be read as running more trials.

entries.complaint: high: "Stop there" is the option for EPANET's UNBALANCED STOP, and the batch itself proves it is ambiguous: the shipped tip (lpn_settings_unbalanced_tip) says stopping 'reports the last trial as it stands', while the code fallback beside this key still reads 'Report nothing' (js/looped-network.js:23195). Two authors read the same two words in opposite ways. The wrong reading tells the user their unconverged numbers are discarded when they are in fact displayed, which is the same class of hazard lpn_diag_not_converged_drawn exists to warn about.
readings: stop at the trial limit and report the last, unconverged trial (intended, EPANET STOP)
stop and report nothing at all (the code's own fallback wording)
stop the run before it reaches the trial limit
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'Stop there' is now 'Stop and report the last trial', which is what the toolkit does. The JS fallback beside it still said 'Report nothing', the opposite; it now matches. dev/ROADMAP.md's note on this label was updated too.

entries.complaint: medium: "Keep trying" is open on WHAT bounds the trying. Its own tip says it allows the extra trials set in the box below, i.e. a bounded number; 'keep trying' reads as unbounded, which on a non-converging network is a promise the page cannot keep and a user will not risk. Its sibling 'Stop there' is separately ambiguous, so the pair cannot disambiguate each other.
readings: allow the extra trials set below, then report (intended, EPANET CONTINUE n)
go on trying with no limit
retry the whole run from the start
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'Keep trying' is now 'Allow extra trials', parallel with its sibling and bounded, which is what EPANET's CONTINUE n does. Its JS fallback ('Report the last try') was also wrong and now matches.

entries.complaint: medium: The tip names the two options with words that appear on neither of them: 'Keeping on' for 'Keep trying' and 'stopping' for 'Stop there'. A translator handles the three strings as three independent units and the tie is lost in every language. Separately, 'which often reaches convergence' has two candidate subjects (the extra trials, or the network), and 'which is close but not a solution' asserts closeness that is not guaranteed for a diverging network.
readings: 'Keeping on' = the Keep trying option (intended) vs a general description of persistence
'which often reaches convergence' - the extra trials do (intended) vs the network does
'close but not a solution' as a guarantee of nearness vs as a caution
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'What to do with a network that has used up its trials and still has not converged. Allowing extra trials often reaches convergence. Stopping reports the last trial as it stands, which is not a solution. Only the EPANET solver reads this box. The built-in solver always stops and marks the answer as not converged.' The tip now names the two options with the words that are on them.

entries.complaint: medium: "Extra trials first" - 'first' floats. It is meant as 'before the last trial is reported', but with no second element named it reads as ordering ('do these before the maximum trials') or as priority. The tip has to supply the missing half, which is what makes the label ambiguous standing alone in a settings row.
readings: extra trials allowed BEFORE the result is reported (intended)
extra trials run BEFORE the maximum trials, i.e. first in sequence
the first of several extra-trial settings
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'Extra trials first' is now 'Extra trials before reporting', which names the second element 'first' was floating against.

entries.complaint: medium: "the largest head any one pipe is still out by" - 'out by' is a British idiom for 'in error by' and does not survive word-for-word rendering; 'out' is separately readable as excluded, or as out of service, both of which are live senses on a page with an active/inactive flag. EPANET's own name for this quantity is head loss error, and its sibling (lpn_settings_flow_change_tip) states its quantity plainly as 'the maximum change in', so the two are not parallel.
readings: the largest remaining head imbalance in any one pipe (intended)
the largest head of any pipe that is left out of the solve
'out by' misparsed as a phrasal verb meaning excluded
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'the largest head any one pipe is still out by' is now 'the largest head error remaining in any one pipe'. The British idiom is gone, so is the excluded/out-of-service reading, and it is now parallel with its sibling lpn_settings_flow_change_tip.

entries.complaint: high: "Zero means it never does." The elided verb phrase can attach to either of the two verbs in the preceding sentence: 'begins taking smaller steps' (intended) or 'converge', which is the nearer one and ends the sentence. The wrong attachment yields 'zero means the network never converges', a false statement about a setting whose shipped default IS zero (js/looped-network.js:22102), so it would tell every default user their network can never converge.
readings: zero means the solver never starts damping (intended)
zero means the network never converges (false, and the setting's default is zero)
zero means the accuracy is never reached
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'Zero means it never does' is now 'Zero means the solver never damps', so it cannot attach to 'converge'. The wrong attachment would have told every default user (the shipped default IS zero) that their network can never converge. 'swinging back and forth' becomes 'oscillating'.

entries.complaint: medium: "One scale on every demand in the network at once." 'Scale' as a countable noun is a graduated rule, a map scale, or a weighing machine - all of which are live on a page that draws a map with a scale bar. The intended sense is a single multiplying factor, which the label itself says ('Demand multiplier'), so the tip's first sentence works against its own label. Second, 'more or less than today's use' leaves 'today' between the calendar day and the present era.
readings: a single multiplying factor applied to every demand at once (intended)
a scale in the map-scale or graduated-rule sense
'today's use' = present-day demand (intended) vs demand on the current date
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'A single factor applied to every demand in the network at once. Use it to ask what the system does at more or less than present-day use. It does not change the numbers you typed. A scenario can carry its own, so average day, maximum day and peak hour are one number each; leave it blank in a scenario to use the project's.' 'One scale' becomes 'A single factor', matching its own label, and 'today's use' becomes 'present-day use'.

entries.complaint: medium: "pulled onto the nearest round angle" - 'round angle' is a defined term in geometry meaning a full 360-degree turn, and several languages have a standing translation for it (es angulo completo, fr angle plein). The intended sense is a whole-number or standard increment. A translator who knows the geometric term writes a sentence saying leader lines snap to 360 degrees. Secondly 'Keep dragging and it lets go' is idiomatic; 'it' is the snap, not the label.
readings: a standard increment such as a multiple of 15 or 45 degrees (intended)
a round angle in the geometric sense, i.e. 360 degrees
a rounded, i.e. curved, corner
entries.resolution: English fixed in both keys. The label is now 'Snap leader lines to set angles' and the tip says 'the nearest of the set angles'; 'round angle' is a defined geometric term meaning 360 degrees with a standing translation in several languages. 'it lets go' is now 'the snap lets go'.

entries.complaint: medium: One key, two selects, two senses. It is the 'no legend' option of the legend-position select (js/looped-network.js:20757) and the 'no snapping' option of the leader-snap angle select (js/looped-network.js:21772, where the siblings are degree numbers). English 'Off' covers both; many languages do not - Spanish would want 'Ninguno' for a position list and 'Desactivado' for a switch, and a translator shown one string must pick one and be wrong in the other select.
readings: switched off / disabled (the snap select)
none / nowhere / hidden (the legend-position select)
'off' in the positional sense, i.e. off the edge of the map
entries.resolution: English fixed BY SPLITTING THE KEY, in full. lpn_settings_legend_off is now 'None' for the legend-position list; a new lpn_settings_legend-sibling key lpn_settings_snap_off ('Off') serves the leader-snap angle list. Call site moved (js/looped-network.js), pageConfig line added (Looped-Network.php), and the code comment that argued for the reuse now records why it was split. No synonym could have been right in both selects.

entries.complaint: low: "so there is one moment to show" omits the 'only' that carries the meaning. Without it the clause states a fact rather than a limitation, and a translator has no cue that this is the reason the transport controls are inert.
readings: there is only one moment to show, so there is nothing to scrub through (intended)
there is a moment available to show
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'so there is one moment to show' is now 'so there is only one moment to show', which is the limitation the transport controls are inert for.

entries.complaint: high: The last sentence tells the reader to press a button that does not exist under that name. lib/lang.ec.en.php sets lpn_time_run to 'Calculate', so the toolbar control is Calculate; the only control on this page whose face reads 'Run' is the fire flow dialog's own button (lpn_ff_calculate).
