A translator translating this key alone has no way to know that 'Run' is meant to be the same word as another key's value, so 26 languages will each invent a third word for a control that is already named.
readings: press the toolbar Calculate button (intended)
press the Run button in the Fire flow dialog
run is a generic verb here and names no control at all
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'Water quality is carried along the pipes over time, so it needs the EPANET engine and a total run time. Set a Total run time under Time, then press the Calculate button.' The toolbar control is Calculate (lpn_time_run); the only face reading 'Run' is the fire-flow dialog's own button, so the old sentence pointed at the wrong control.

entries.complaint: medium: Same cross-key dependency, in the string that is right beside the button. 'Press Calculate' is only correct as long as lpn_time_run keeps the value 'Calculate', and a translator sees neither key from inside this one. Separately, 'the results for the later times are not kept up to date while you work' reads two ways.
readings: later times were computed once and have since gone stale (intended)
later times are never computed at all until you press the button
Calculate is an ordinary verb, not the name of a control
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'Press Calculate' is now 'Press the Calculate button', which is the convention that marks it as a control name; lpn_time_run supplies the word. The stale-results clause is unchanged: it is accurate and the second reading ('never computed at all') is closed by 'not kept up to date'.

entries.complaint: medium: The tip on the Calculate button names a different time step from the note under it. This string says 'all hydraulic time steps'; lpn_time_run_note says 'the first reporting time'. Those are two distinct EPANET quantities (Hydraulic time step and Report time step, both of which this page exposes as separate settings) and a translator reading the pair will reasonably assume they are the same thing said twice and unify them. 'for' is also ambiguous between duration and enumeration.
readings: solve at each hydraulic time step, over the whole duration (intended)
solve for the length of time covered by the hydraulic steps
produce a result at every reporting time
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'Solve this network at every hydraulic time step, from the start of the run to the end of it.' It names the hydraulic time step as the WORK and leaves reporting times to the note, so the two strings no longer look like one thing said twice.

entries.complaint: medium: A two-word Settings section heading with no verb, over controls that set what a NEWLY DRAWN element starts with. 'Asset' is a genuine water-utility term (asset management) and also the ordinary software word for files and images, and 'New assets' with no article can be read as an instruction to make some.
readings: defaults applied to assets you create from now on (intended)
a command or link that adds new assets
assets in the file sense: images, tiles, resources
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'New assets' is now 'Defaults for new assets'. The imperative reading and the software-resource reading are both gone. NOT 'elements' as proposed: asset is the 44-to-7 incumbent and finding 66 in this same pass argued the other way, so the pass had to pick one, and incumbency picks asset.

entries.complaint: medium: A one-word control label that is a verb and a noun in English and is neither in most target languages. Nothing in the string says a choice is being made or what is being tracked; the sibling values are noun phrases (Water age, Source trace), so the label and its options are different parts of speech, which is the exact defect that broke lpn_settings_text_size_map in sprint 241.
readings: what the water quality run should follow through the network (intended)
an imperative: track this network
a noun: the track, the path, the route
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'Track' is now 'Quality parameter', EPANET's own name for this selector and a noun phrase parallel with its values.

entries.complaint: medium: 'Neither one asks you for any other number' is true only in the narrowest reading. Choosing Source trace immediately requires the Trace node control below it, which is another input; it is a node rather than a number, so the sentence is defensible and also actively misleading, and no translator can tell which reading was intended. 'trace' here is also the ordinary verb while 'Source trace' one row down is the name of one of the two options.
readings: neither option needs a further NUMBER typed, though one needs a node picked (intended)
neither option needs any further input at all, which is false for Source trace
trace here is the same thing as the option called Source trace
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'Choose what the run should follow through the pipes: how long the water has been in the system, or where it came from. Neither one needs a concentration or a reaction rate.' 'trace' as an ordinary verb becomes 'follow' so it stops colliding with the Source trace option, and the false-in-one-reading denial is replaced by the true thing: no chemistry input is needed, and the Trace node is not denied.

entries.complaint: medium: The label above it says 'node' and the tip says 'point' twice. A translator will render them as two different words, so the tip stops naming the thing the label names. 'came from here' has no unambiguous antecedent inside the string.
readings: point means the trace node named by the label (intended)
point is any location on the map, not necessarily a node
here means this setting rather than the traced node
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'The node whose water is traced. Every other node then shows the share of its water that came from that node.' 'point' becomes 'node' twice, matching the label above it, and 'here' is replaced.

entries.complaint: medium: A dropdown value carrying a parenthetical sentence, both halves of which are elliptical. 'kept' has no object, and 'worked out' is the page's house verb for computed, which a translator is as likely to read as understood or figured out. The stake is real: the wrong reading tells a user that a chemical analysis was run when it was not.
readings: the chemical named in the imported file is preserved in the document but is not simulated (intended)
the chemical selection is kept but has not been figured out yet
kept refers to the option staying selected
entries.resolution: English fixed. '(kept, not worked out)' is now '(stored, not calculated)'. 'Calculated' is the word on this page's own Calculate button, and the understood/figured-out reading is gone.

entries.complaint: high: The defining sentence of the demand result has two arithmetics in it and only one is right. 'the total of base demands multiplied by their patterns' parses as (sum of the base demands) x (their patterns) as readily as sum of (each base demand x its own pattern). These give different numbers whenever a junction has more than one demand category, which is exactly the case this tip exists to explain.
readings: the sum over categories of base demand times that category's pattern multiplier (intended)
the total base demand, then multiplied by the patterns
the total of the base demands, and separately the total of their patterns
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'The flow this node draws at the time step shown: each base demand multiplied by its own pattern, added together. It is calculated, not typed, so it changes with the clock and cannot be edited.' The arithmetic is now unambiguous: each base demand times its own pattern, added together. The two parses give different numbers exactly when a junction has more than one demand category, which is the case the tip exists for.

entries.complaint: high: 'Leave it at No pattern to use the project's specified default pattern' is self-contradicting on its face: it tells you to select no pattern in order to get a pattern. 'No pattern' is also a control VALUE defined by another key, invisible from here, and 'specified default' is two adjectives where EPANET has one named option (Default Pattern in Analysis Options). A translator who resolves it the natural way writes 'leave it blank and no pattern is applied', which is a false statement about what the model does.
readings: selecting No pattern makes the junction fall back to the project's Default Pattern (intended)
selecting No pattern means the demand is constant and no pattern applies
specified default pattern means whichever pattern happens to be first
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'How this junction’s demand rises and falls through the run. Leave it at No pattern and the junction follows the project’s Default Pattern instead.' The self-contradiction ('select no pattern to get a pattern') is resolved into a fallback statement, and 'specified default pattern' becomes EPANET's named Default Pattern.

entries.complaint: medium: One word, 'Description', doing duty as the heading of the demand-category column AND as a searchable node property in Find and replace (js/looped-network.js line 8012), where it sits in a list of node properties with no demand context at all. Read there, it plainly means the description OF THE NODE. Its own tip then says 'the category', a word the label never introduces.
readings: the description of one demand category at this junction (intended)
a description of the node itself
a free-text note attached to the row
entries.resolution: English fixed on the TIP only. The column heading stays 'Description', which is Tom's own word as of Task 553 and answers in Find and replace too. lpn_field_demand_category_tip now reads 'Name or description of this demand category.', so the tip names the category the label leaves to context instead of introducing a word from nowhere.

entries.complaint: medium: The button says 'Add demand category' and its own tip says 'Add another demand at this junction'. Two nouns for one action, in strings a translator reads side by side, so at least one language will conclude they are different operations. EPANET's term is demand category and should win.
readings: add another demand category row (intended)
add a classification to an existing demand
add a demand, which the tip calls something else
entries.resolution: English fixed on the TIP, not the label: the label keeps EPANET's own 'Add demand category' and lpn_demand_add_tip now reads 'Add another demand category at this junction, with its own base demand, pattern and description. The categories add up.', so the two strings a translator reads side by side name one operation.

entries.complaint: high: A confirmation prompt for an action that types into the user's document, and the object of 'Replace' is elided while '{n}' is a bare number. 'Replace those {n} with Mapbox DEM' most literally says the NODES are being replaced by a DEM. Nothing inside the string names elevations, and this is the one string standing between a user and 30 m data overwriting their numbers.
readings: replace the elevation of those n nodes with values read from the Mapbox DEM (intended)
replace those n nodes themselves with a DEM layer
replace those n elevation values with the Mapbox DEM as a data source setting
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'Replace the elevation of those {n} nodes with values from the Mapbox DEM?' The object of 'Replace' is named, which matters on the one string standing between a user and 30 m data typed into their document.

entries.complaint: medium: 'the nodes that will be filled in' says the NODES are filled, not their elevations. In a drawing application 'filled in' is also what happens to a shape, and this string is read next to a map. Same shape in lpn_terrain_filled_ids.
readings: these nodes will have their elevation written from the DEM (intended)
these nodes will be drawn filled or shaded
these nodes will be completed in some unspecified way
entries.resolution: English fixed in both siblings: 'These nodes will get an elevation: {ids}' and 'These nodes got an elevation: {ids}'. The elevation, not the node, is what gets filled.

entries.complaint: medium: 'still blank' has no noun. A node is not blank; its elevation is. A translator with no antecedent in the string will attach blankness to the node, which in a map editor reads as unlabelled or empty rather than missing a number.
readings: these nodes still have no elevation (intended)
these nodes are empty or unnamed
these nodes were not drawn
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'These nodes are still blank' is now 'These nodes still have no elevation', which supplies the noun blankness was attaching to.

entries.complaint: medium: 'They are: {ids}' is pure anaphora with the antecedent in a different key (lpn_terrain_keep, which is not in this batch). Every gendered language must choose a gender and number for 'they' with nothing to choose from, and the two candidates in the surrounding paragraph are nodes and elevations.
readings: the nodes that already have an elevation and will not be touched (intended)
the elevations that will be kept
the nodes that will be filled in, if the reader misattaches the sentence
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'They are: {ids}' is now 'Those nodes are: {ids}', so no gendered language has to choose an antecedent that is in a different key.

entries.complaint: medium: 'better than a metre across the ground and a few tenths of a metre up and down' is the string's only statement of what accuracy means, and it invents a phrasing for two quantities that already have names. 'Across the ground' can be horizontal position, horizontal resolution or ground sample distance, and a reader deciding whether to trust a DEM for a pipe profile needs the vertical number specifically.
readings: about 1 m horizontal and a few tenths of a metre vertical accuracy (intended)
1 m ground resolution, i.e. pixel size, with a separate vertical figure
accuracy measured along the ground surface, as opposed to along the line of sight
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'across the ground' and 'up and down' are now 'horizontally' and 'vertically' in both pairs. The two em dashes went with the rewrite (the 3DEP clause is now a 'such as ... and ...' aside), so the ratchet baseline falls from 69 to 64 across this pass.

entries.complaint: medium: Two problems in one sentence. 'its residual pressure' reads as a property the junction has, when it is a criterion the user typed into the dialog; and 'Test every junction' is false whenever the scope is set to the selected junction only, which is one of the two values of the very first control in that dialog.
readings: hold the residual pressure you specified for the run (intended)
hold the residual pressure that this junction has
every junction is always tested, with no choice of scope
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'Test junctions one at a time: how much can each deliver while still holding the residual pressure you set, and does drawing the required flow there push anything else out of limits?' 'Test every junction' becomes 'Test junctions one at a time', which is true under both scopes, and the residual is named as the criterion the user set rather than a property the junction has.

entries.complaint: medium: 'your code' is a polysemy trap of the first order. Standing alone in a hydraulics tool it is as readable as software code or a postal/area code as it is as a fire code, and several target languages have no word that covers the regulatory sense without a qualifier. 'at a hydrant' also floats: it can qualify the flow or the requirement.
readings: the fire code that applies to your project (intended)
a code you wrote, a program
a reference code or number identifying something
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'your code' is now 'your fire code', which closes the software-code and area-code readings in the one place the word appears alone.

entries.complaint: medium: 'this junction alone must provide' has two readings and one of them is a claim about hydraulics, not about scope. It means 'this junction in particular', but reads just as naturally as 'this junction unaided', which would be a statement that no other part of the network contributes. The second sentence also names 'the Fire flow box', a control whose visible label is 'Required fire flow'.
readings: the requirement that applies to this junction in particular (intended)
the flow this junction must supply without help from the rest of the system
the flow available at this junction on its own
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'The fire flow required at this particular junction, from your fire code or your fire authority for the land use it serves. Leave it blank and the junction is tested against the number in the Required fire flow box.' 'this junction alone must provide' becomes 'required at this particular junction' (the unaided reading was a false claim about the hydraulics), and the box is named by its visible label, Required fire flow.

entries.complaint: high: As written, the tip's subject is the wrong quantity. '20 psi is the ... convention for available fire flow' says 20 psi IS a fire flow, which is a category error a translator will faithfully reproduce; and it never says what the number is for, which is the residual pressure held while the available flow is measured. It also hardcodes psi in a field whose unit selector may be showing kPa or bar, with no SI value beside it.
readings: 20 psi is the residual pressure conventionally held when measuring available fire flow (intended)
20 psi is the conventional required fire flow
20 psi is the pressure at which fire flow becomes available
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'The pressure the junction must still hold while delivering the fire flow. AWWA M31 and NFPA 291 use 20 psi (140 kPa).' The subject was the wrong quantity: 20 psi is the residual pressure, not a fire flow. The SI equivalent is given beside it because the field's unit selector may be showing kPa or bar.

entries.complaint: medium: 'Design check (effect on system)' names the whole system where the check deliberately excludes the junction under test, and the JS fallback beside it says 'Effect on the rest of the system'. 'Design check' can also be read as the name of the result rather than of the setting, which matters because this label sits on a selector whose values are 'Do not check' and two scopes.
readings: choose whether, and over what set, to check the effect on the REST of the system (intended)
a check of the design of the system as a whole, this junction included
the design check result
entries.resolution: Dismissed. The label is Tom's own, verbatim and dated 2026-09-02: *"Most software has the word Design, doesn't it? Should we put 'Design check (effect on system)'?"* -- the profession's word first, the plain gloss in the bracket. Rewriting his bracket the same day is not a Wave 0 finding's call.

entries.complaint: medium: 'run too fast' uses 'run' for fluid velocity on a page where Run and Runs are already the names of a control and a results column. A translator who has just rendered the Runs heading will read this as something about the analysis running.
readings: exceed the velocity limit you set (intended)
take too long / execute too quickly, i.e. about the analysis
operate outside its design condition generally
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'run too fast' is now 'exceed its velocity limit', off the Run/Runs collision.

entries.complaint: medium: 'Every other junction' is one of the best known ambiguities in English: each of the remaining ones, or alternating ones. As a scope selector for a design check, the wrong reading changes what the report is understood to cover, and the string carries no context that rules it out.
readings: all junctions except the one being tested (intended)
every second junction, alternating
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'Every other junction' is now 'All other junctions', removing the alternating reading.

entries.complaint: medium: Same 'every other' ambiguity as lpn_ff_design_nodes, compounded because 'every pipe' beside it is unambiguously distributive, which invites the reader to hunt for a contrast in 'every other'.
readings: all other junctions and all pipes (intended)
every second junction, and every pipe
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now 'All other junctions and all pipes', same reason.

entries.complaint: medium: Two words carry the sentence and both are traps. 'its lateral' is US water-industry shorthand for the service or hydrant lateral and is a bare adjective in most languages; and 'it is the usual one' is a claim about practice sitting next to 'That is the method used here', so the two sentences can be read as one claim or two.
readings: the hydrant lateral pipe is not modelled (intended)
lateral as a direction: sideways losses
the usual one refers to the hydrant rather than to the method
entries.resolution: English fixed in the half that was a trap. 'its lateral' is now 'its lateral pipe', so the bare adjective has its noun. The two-sentence structure stays: 'That is the method used here, and it is the usual one' is a Tom-driven wording (2026-08-30, after he read a version that led with the absence), and the loss accounting has to lead with what the tool DOES.

entries.complaint: high: Two sentences, and the reader cannot tell whether the second describes what this tool did or what the reader should do. 'Fire flow is normally added to maximum day demand' is advice about practice, printed directly under a statement about the run, so it reads as a description of the run itself. A user who takes that reading believes the sweep was made at maximum day demand when it was made at whatever time step is on screen, and reports a fire flow that was never tested.
readings: standard practice is max day demand, so set that condition yourself before running (intended)
this run adds the fire flow to maximum day demand
maximum day demand is normally added on top of the fire flow
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'Only the time step now on screen is tested. Fire flow is normally tested on top of maximum day demand, so set the network to that condition before you run.' The second sentence now plainly instructs rather than describing, so nobody can read it as a claim that the sweep was made at maximum day demand.

entries.complaint: medium: 'What is below is what had already been worked out' uses 'below' spatially in a document whose contents are pressures and flows, where below is a magnitude. It is also a headless relative clause twice over, which several target languages cannot mirror without inventing a noun.
readings: the results shown further down the page are the ones already finished (intended)
the results under some threshold value are the finished ones
what remains is what had been computed, i.e. the rest was discarded
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'Stopped after {done} of {total} junctions. The results below are the ones already finished.' The two headless relative clauses become one noun phrase, and 'below' is unambiguously the page.

entries.complaint: medium: '{solves} network runs.' is a bare noun phrase punctuated as a sentence, with no verb to tell a translator whether it is a report of what happened, a forecast, or a heading. 'Runs' is also the plural noun of the page's Calculate action rather than of any control named Run.
readings: this sweep took N solves of the whole network (intended)
N network runs will be needed
a label meaning number of network runs
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'This run solved the whole network {solves} times.' Verified at the call site (js/looped-network.js, set.solves after the run): it reports what happened, so it is now a sentence that says so.

entries.complaint: medium: Three sentences, each beginning with a bare number and no noun. Translators must supply the noun (junctions) to inflect anything, and they cannot see it. Worse, the three counts are deliberately NOT exclusive (js/lpn-fireflow.js counts modes independently), so a language that renders them as a partition, which the parallel form invites, states something false about the run.
readings: N junctions had nothing wrong, N failed the fire flow, N affected the rest of the system, and the sets overlap (intended)
the three counts partition the junctions tested
the counts are of something other than junctions, e.g. of checks
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: '{clean} junctions had nothing wrong. {fire} junctions failed the fire flow. {design} junctions affected the rest of the system.' The noun is supplied three times, which was the finding. The proposed overlap sentence was NOT added: this same key drives the LIVE PROGRESS TALLY (js/lpn-fireflow.js, once per junction), so a twelve-word caveat would repeat on every step of a sweep.

entries.complaint: medium: Same headless count, plus 'could not be answered' predicated of junctions rather than of questions. A junction is not answered; its fire flow question is.
readings: N junctions produced no answer (intended)
N questions could not be answered
N junctions did not respond, i.e. a network or engine failure
entries.resolution: English fixed. '{n} could not be answered.' is now '{n} junctions could not be answered.'

entries.complaint: medium: Read as a heading it means 'the junctions that were tested'; read as a sentence, which is how a heading with a past participle scans in several languages, it claims every junction WAS tested. That claim is false when the scope was the selected junction only, and false again past 200 rows, which is the same table's own truncation limit.
readings: the junctions that were tested (intended)
every junction in the project was tested
an instruction: test every junction
entries.resolution: Dismissed. 'Every junction tested' is the heading of the one-table report Tom settled on 2026-08-30, and the truncation and scope caveats it is charged with are already stated in their own strings (lpn_ff_stopped names done-of-total; the scope selector lpn_ff_scope is set before the run). Renaming his heading to fix a reading the report already answers is not worth the 26 retranslations.

entries.complaint: medium: The column reports the pressure at the junction with the network's ordinary demands running and no fire flow drawn. That is the fire-test sense of static pressure and is correct usage, but the general hydraulic sense of static is no flow anywhere, and nothing in the table says which is meant. A reader on the wrong sense treats the number as a no-demand pressure, which is always higher.
readings: pressure before the fire flow is drawn, with normal demands running (intended)
pressure with no flow anywhere in the system
static as in a static, non time varying result
entries.resolution: Glossary. New term 'static pressure (fire flow)', wired to lpn, stating that it is the pressure before any fire flow is drawn WITH the ordinary demands still running, and refusing the no-flow reading, the unchanging reading and the electrical one. The heading stands: AWWA M31 and NFPA 291 both call it static pressure.

entries.complaint: medium: 'Available flow' drops the word that makes it a term of art. In a hydraulic results table beside velocities and pressures, available flow reads as the flow presently available in the pipes. The paired heading lpn_ff_col_required has the same shape and inherits the same reading.
readings: available fire flow: the largest fire flow that still holds the residual (intended)
the flow currently available at this junction
spare capacity in the pipes serving it
entries.resolution: Glossary. New term 'available fire flow', wired to lpn, which names the concept both short headings stand for and says why they are short (column width is king). The headings 'Available flow' and 'Required flow' stand; widening them to four words each is exactly what the results-table rule forbids.

entries.complaint: medium: 'Residual held' is a participle with its condition removed. The cell holds the pressure the junction still had while delivering the available flow, and neither the word pressure nor the flow it was held at is in the string. A translator gets an adjective and a past participle and no noun.
readings: the residual pressure still present at the available flow (intended)
whether the residual criterion was met, i.e. a yes or no
residual as leftover: the flow left over
entries.resolution: Dismissed. The fire flow table's column headings AND their order are Tom's, set 2026-09-01 and 2026-09-02, and 'Available flow' and 'Residual held' are deliberately adjacent because they are one reading -- a flow without the pressure it was held at is a number without its condition. That adjacency is what supplies the missing condition, so the participle is not standing alone on the screen the way it stands alone in a key list.

entries.complaint: medium: 'Pressure at required' ends on an adjective with its noun deleted. English readers recover 'flow' from the neighbouring column; a translator working down a key list has a 50/50 chance of recovering 'required pressure' instead, which inverts the column into the criterion it is being compared against.
readings: the pressure at the junction when the required fire flow is drawn (intended)
the pressure required at the junction
pressure measured at the required condition, unspecified
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'Pressure at required' is now 'Pressure at required flow', so it cannot invert into 'required pressure'.

entries.complaint: high: The heading names one physical effect and the column reports two. ffCriticalText() prints either a junction pulled below the minimum pressure OR a pipe running above the maximum velocity, and a fast pipe is not a drawdown by any reading of the word. 'Drawdown' additionally carries a specific groundwater meaning (decline of a well water level) that most target languages have a dedicated and wrong word for.
readings: the worst thing this junction pulled down or drove too fast (intended)
the drop in pressure at other junctions only
well drawdown, in the groundwater sense
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'Drawdowns' is now 'Worst effect', which is true of both things ffCriticalText() prints: a junction pulled below its minimum pressure OR a pipe above its maximum velocity. A fast pipe is not a drawdown by any reading, and drawdown additionally carries a groundwater sense most target languages have a dedicated wrong word for.

entries.complaint: high: Same error, in a sentence rather than a heading: 'Nothing in the chosen set was drawn down by any junction tested' is printed whenever the effects list is empty, and that list holds over-velocity pipes as well as low-pressure junctions. If any pipe HAD been over velocity the sentence would not print, so as worded the page says nothing about velocity at all while claiming the design check found nothing.
readings: no junction was pushed below the minimum pressure and no pipe above the maximum velocity (intended)
no pressures were reduced, which says nothing about velocities
drawn down in the groundwater sense
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'Nothing in the chosen set went outside its limits while any junction drew its fire flow.' Same error in sentence form: the effects list holds over-velocity pipes too, so the old wording claimed the design check found nothing while saying nothing about velocity.

entries.complaint: medium: The heading says 'Design limit' and the cells say 'Pressure', 'Velocity', 'Pressure and velocity' or 'Not checked'. A limit is a number; these cells are the name of the limit that was broken. Heading and content are different parts of speech, so a translator will render the heading as the numeric criterion and the reader will look for a value.
readings: which design limit was exceeded (intended)
the value of the design limit applied
the limit imposed by the design of the system
entries.resolution: Dismissed on the same ground as the Residual held finding: this table's headings are Tom's own, dated 2026-09-02. 'Design limit' over cells naming which limit was broken is a normal table idiom, and the row's Failure modes cell already says Design when one was.

entries.complaint: medium: 'Static failed' turns an adjective into a bare noun and drops the criterion. Nothing static failed; the junction was already below the residual pressure with no fire flow drawn. 'Static' alone also has an everyday electrical and radio sense that several languages will reach for first.
readings: the static pressure was already below the residual, so nothing further was measured (intended)
a static analysis failed
static as in interference or as in unchanging
entries.resolution: Dismissed. 'Static failed, so not checked' is what Tom asked for on 2026-09-02, choosing a word or two over the bare dash that stood there (*"I agree that a word or two is better"*), and it sits under the 'Static pressure' column that supplies the noun. The proposed longer forms spend the cell width he was economising.

entries.complaint: medium: The heading 'Runs' counts solves of the whole network. On this page 'run' is also the name of an extended period simulation, the fire flow sweep is called a run in three other strings in this same batch, and in waterworks English a run of pipe is a length of it. In a table whose first column is Junction, a reader can plausibly take Runs as pipe runs.
readings: the number of times the whole network was solved for this junction (intended)
the number of simulation runs the project has made
runs of pipe serving the junction
entries.resolution: Dismissed on the same ground: Tom set this table's headings on 2026-09-02, and the glossary already carries 'run (a simulation)' wired to lpn with 'a RUN OF PIPE -- a straight length of main between two points. That sense is live on this very page and is the trap to guard against' at the head of its avoid array. The guard the finding asks for is already delivered.

entries.complaint: medium: A cell containing the single word 'Fire' under the heading 'Failure modes'. It means the junction failed its fire flow criterion. Alone it is the noun for combustion, and every target language will translate the noun. Tom chose the two one-word modes deliberately (2026-09-02), so the English should stand and the translator needs the missing half in the synonym channel.
readings: failed the fire flow criterion (intended)
fire, the thing that burns
a fire condition or fire event
entries.resolution: Glossary. Tom ruled the one-word English stands (2026-09-02), so the missing half now travels in the wired 'fire flow' term, whose context states that the Failure modes column prints 'Fire' for a junction that did not deliver its required fire flow and 'Design' for one that pushed something else outside its limits, and that both are shortened verdicts to be kept short. PROPOSAL LEFT UNWRITTEN (AI may not touch $ec_lang_syn): $ec_lang_syn['lpn_ff_mode_fire']='Fire flow, Fire flow failure, Did not deliver the required fire flow. | layout: column heading; avoid: fire as combustion'.

entries.complaint: medium: 'Design' alone in a cell, meaning the junction's fire flow pushed something else outside its design limits. As a bare word it is a noun and a verb and names an activity rather than a failure.
readings: failed the design check: something else went outside its limits (intended)
the design of the network
an imperative or an activity
entries.resolution: Glossary. Same extended 'fire flow' term as finding 127 carries this cell too. English stands on Tom's ruling. PROPOSAL LEFT UNWRITTEN (AI may not touch $ec_lang_syn): $ec_lang_syn['lpn_ff_mode_design']='Design check, Design limit failure, Pushed another asset outside its design limits. | layout: column heading'.

entries.complaint: medium: 'over {flow}' is two words with no verb, printed in the Available fire flow cell when the search hit its ceiling. 'Over' is one of the most overloaded prepositions in English and none of its senses is marked here: greater than, across, during, or finished.
readings: more than {flow}: the search ceiling was reached and the residual still held (intended)
over as in during or across a period
over as in finished, the run ended at that flow
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'over {flow}' is now 'more than {flow}', which is the only sense of 'over' that was meant.

entries.complaint: medium: '{id} down to {pressure}' is telegraphic and verbless. 'Down to' can mean reduced to, or as far as, or attributable to, and the last of those makes the cell read as an explanation of blame rather than a measurement. The companion lpn_ff_affect_link ('{id} at {velocity}') has the same problem in milder form.
readings: junction {id} was pulled down to {pressure} (intended)
the effect goes as far as {id}, at pressure {pressure}
it comes down to {id}, i.e. {id} is the cause
entries.resolution: English fixed in both siblings: '{id} drops to {pressure}' and '{id} reaches {velocity}'. Both now carry a verb, and 'down to' is gone with its attributable-to reading.

entries.complaint: high: ONE string, TWO different nouns, which CLAUDE.md forbids by name (reuse stops at sentences; a shared string must be true of all its uses). js/looped-network.js appends it to the Drawdowns cell where {n} counts affected junctions and pipes, and again as the line under the table where {n} counts junctions not printed. Every gendered or case-marking language must pick one noun to agree with, so one of the two call sites will be wrong in most of the 26.
readings: and n more affected elements (call site 1)
and n more junctions not shown (call site 2)
and n more of whatever the reader last saw
entries.resolution: English fixed BY SPLITTING THE KEY, in full. lpn_ff_more is now 'and {n} more affected' for the Worst effect cell; a new lpn_ff_rows_more, '{n} more junctions are not shown.', serves the line under the table. Call site moved (js/looped-network.js ffMoreLine), pageConfig line added (Looped-Network.php), and a comment at the split says why. One string counting two different nouns is what CLAUDE.md forbids by name.

entries.complaint: high: 'ISO' here is the Insurance Services Office, a US fire insurance rating organisation. Worldwide, and to every one of the 26 translators, ISO means the International Organization for Standardization, which publishes no fire flow hydrant credit. Nothing in the string disambiguates it, so the sentence will be translated as an international standard and read as one, which is a false attribution printed on a deliverable.
readings: the Insurance Services Office, the US fire insurance rating body (intended)
the International Organization for Standardization
an ISO standard number that was omitted
entries.resolution: English fixed. Now: 'The Insurance Services Office (ISO) credits a single hydrant with at most {flow}. That credit limit has not been applied here because we do not know how many hydrants a node may represent.' The acronym is expanded, so nobody translates the US Insurance Services Office as the International Organization for Standardization on a deliverable.

entries.complaint: high: 'with nothing drawn' is false on its face: the network's ordinary demands are still running, and only the fire flow is absent. The key's own name says at_rest, which points at the same wrong idea. A user reading it as no demand at all concludes the network cannot hold the residual even empty, which is a far more alarming diagnosis than the true one.
readings: already below the residual before any FIRE FLOW is drawn, with normal demands running (intended)
already below the residual with no demand at all anywhere
at rest meaning the network is not being simulated
entries.resolution: English fixed. 'Already below the residual with nothing drawn' is now 'Already below the residual before any fire flow is drawn'. The old wording was false on its face (the ordinary demands are still running) and produced a far more alarming diagnosis than the true one. The JS fallback moved with it; the key name still says at_rest and is left alone, since renaming it is rename_lang_key.php work with no reader benefit.

entries.complaint: medium: The placeholder is named {id} and holds a solver ERROR CODE (js/looped-network.js substitutes rec.code). Every other {id} in this batch holds an element name, so a translator who reasons about the placeholder, as several have in past sprints, will write a sentence about a node. 'the reason given' also leaves the giver unnamed on a page with two engines.
readings: no answer, and the code the solver reported is {id} (intended)
no answer, and the element responsible is {id}
no answer, and the reason we gave is {id}
entries.resolution: English fixed AND the placeholder renamed. The string is now 'No answer. The code reported was {code}.' and js/looped-network.js substitutes into {code}. Every other {id} in this report holds an asset name, which is what a translator reasoning about the token would have written about.

entries.complaint: low: The four state words (Passing, Failing, Design issue, No answer) are present participles or fragments with no subject, and 'Passing' in particular reads as passing THROUGH as readily as meeting a criterion. Worth noting separately: ffStateText() is defined at js/looped-network.js line 27619 and is called from nowhere, and lpn_ff_col_result appears in Looped-Network.php's pageConfig but in no renderer. These five keys currently reach no screen, so the sprint would pay 5 x 26 translations for text nobody sees.
readings: meets the criteria (intended)
passing through, in transit
acceptable or adequate, i.e. only just passing
entries.resolution: Keys DELETED, English-only, nothing paid. Verified: ffStateText() (js/looped-network.js) was defined once and called from nowhere, and lpn_ff_col_result appeared only in Looped-Network.php's pageConfig; the fire-flow table replaced its Result column with Failure modes. Deleted: lpn_ff_col_result, lpn_ff_state_pass, lpn_ff_state_fail, lpn_ff_state_design, lpn_ff_state_error, plus the dead function and the five pageConfig lines. None of the five existed in any of the 26 other language files, so the sprint no longer pays 5 x 26 translations for text that reaches no screen.

entries.complaint: The English query grammar uses a capitalized keyword AND that visually stands apart from surrounding words. The natural Arabic word for "and" is the single letter و, which in ordinary Arabic is usually attached directly to the following word as a prefix rather than standing alone. Used as a bare query keyword between two conditions it may read as a stray letter or a typo rather than a recognizable operator, unlike English AND. I translated it literally (و) per the glossary's instruction to translate query keywords, but flag this as a case where the literal translation may hurt scanability of the query line.
readings: Translate literally as و (chosen)
Keep AND untranslated in Arabic since both forms are accepted by the parser
entries.resolution: Same answer as lpn_find_q_err_dot: findAlts() accepts the translated token and the English one, so AND/OR may be localized without breaking a query anybody has already written.

entries.complaint: This tip's English says the junction falls back to "the project's Default Pattern", but the actual setting the user sees is labelled lpn_settings_default_pattern = "Default demand pattern" (lowercase, different wording, not capitalized as a proper control-name reference). Per the control-name rule I translated the tip to match the real control label, but the English source itself does not name the control by its literal words, so every translator has to make this same judgment call independently.
readings: Match the real control label 'Default demand pattern' (chosen)
Translate 'Default Pattern' literally as if it were its own distinct control
entries.resolution: Correct catch: the tip named 'the project's Default Pattern' while the control's own key lpn_settings_default_pattern reads 'Default demand pattern'. The agent matched the real control label per the control-name rule, which is what the rule is for.

entries.complaint: The glossary's preferred_translation for 'emitter' is 'капкоотделител', but the sibling key lpn_settings_emitter_exponent (not stale, already shipped) already renders 'emitter' as 'дюза' ('nozzle') in the field label 'Степенен показател на дюзата'. I translated this tip to match the label already on screen ('дюза'), since a tip that named the control differently from its own label would point at nothing. A future sprint should decide whether to rename the existing label to match the glossary's капкоотделител (a rename_lang_key.php-scale change) or update the glossary to record дюза as the incumbent for bg.
readings: дюза, matching the sibling label already shipped (chosen)
капкоотделител, matching the glossary's preferred_translation but breaking consistency with the on-screen label
entries.resolution: The agents were right and the glossary was wrong. Its emitter renderings are the IRRIGATION dripper (ru kapelnitsa reads as an intravenous drip; bn and bg likewise), while each of those files already had a settled lpn_ incumbent across a dozen shipped keys. All three kept the incumbent against the entry's advice, which is the correct call; the entry now carries that correction and tells a future agent to prefer the EPANET sense for an lpn_ string.

entries.complaint: The value 'Mapbox DEM' is a product name plus an acronym with no established Bulgarian rendering, so I kept it byte-identical to English -- the only defensible choice, since inventing a Cyrillic acronym would be worse than the English one. dev/scripts/lang_syntax_validate.php --lang=bg flags this as [identical-to-english] because the key is not listed in dev/scripts/translation_exempt_keys.json, and I cannot edit that file (my brief restricts me to lib/lang.ec.bg.php only). The orchestrator should add lpn_settings_elev_source_dem (and probably lpn_elev_dem_said, which also carries the literal 'Mapbox DEM' string mid-sentence, though that one is not flagged since it is not byte-identical as a whole value) to translation_exempt_keys.json.
readings: Leave 'Mapbox DEM' identical across every language and add the key to translation_exempt_keys.json (chosen, but needs the orchestrator's file access)
Invent a transliterated or translated form with no real-world referent, which would mislead a reader searching Mapbox's own documentation
entries.resolution: Answered by a DECLARATION, not by wording: the key is now in dev/scripts/translation_exempt_keys.json as a product name. Exemption says identical to English is ALLOWED, never required, so bg keeps the bare 'Mapbox DEM' it refused to dodge and the languages that built a natural phrase around the two words (am's genitive, sw's 'DEM ya Mapbox', km's 'Mapbox DEM layer') keep those. The bg agent was the one that named the real problem instead of working around it; five others had already reached for a word order chosen only to differ from English in bytes.

entries.complaint: This button's English label is 'Run', while the pre-existing lpn_time_run key (the Time panel's button) is labelled 'Calculate' and already translated 'Изчисли'. Nothing in the payload states whether the two English words name the same action in two places (both trigger a solve) or are deliberately distinct words for distinct actions (one loops over every junction, the other advances the clock). I translated both as 'Изчисли', treating 'Run' and 'Calculate' as synonyms throughout the suite, since Bulgarian has no established shorter word for a fire-flow-specific 'Run' that would not read as a mistranslation of 'Calculate'.
readings: Изчисли for both, treating Run and Calculate as the same user-facing action (chosen)
A distinct word such as 'Пусни' for lpn_ff_calculate, to keep the two buttons visibly different even though their English words already look interchangeable
entries.resolution: Not a synonym pair and the English stands: lpn_time_run ('Calculate') solves the network, and lpn_ff_calculate ('Run') starts the fire flow sweep, which is a different action taking minutes rather than milliseconds. Keeping them visibly distinct, as de, bn and bg each chose to, is right. Recorded here because three agents had to reason it out from scratch.

entries.complaint: EPANET 'tags' (asset metadata strings, lpn_inp_drop_tags) is a concept with no glossary entry and no prior bg rendering. It is a different thing from a map Label (this suite's own vocabulary, already lpn_labels_* = 'етикет') and from a Text object ('текст'), so reusing either word would collide with an existing, unrelated concept. I coined 'таг' (a common Bulgarian IT loanword, distinct from 'етикет') for this sprint's three lpn_inp_drop_tags-adjacent sentences. Since the feature it describes ('no place on this page to see a tag yet') is explicitly not yet built, this word has no on-screen counterpart to check against and may need revisiting once a Tags UI ships.
readings: таг, an IT loanword kept distinct from етикет=Label and текст=Text (chosen)
маркер, a native Bulgarian word for 'marker/tag', also unused elsewhere in this file
entries.resolution: Added 'tag (EPANET)' to glossary.json and wired it to the lpn prefix. Its avoid list names the collision all four agents found on their own: the natural word for a tag is the word this suite already spends on its own Label object. The recommended handling is the one they each chose independently, to borrow the English word or use a data-field term, never the Label word.

entries.complaint: The 'fire flow' glossary entry says to prefer a language's own settled fire-protection term where one exists, but I have no way to confirm from the payload alone what Bangladeshi or Indian water-utility fire-protection practice actually calls this quantity. I coined 'অগ্নিনির্বাপণ প্রবাহ' (literally 'fire-suppression flow') consistently across the whole Fire flow feature, since this feature is entirely new to the Bengali file and there was no incumbent term anywhere else in lib/lang.ec.bn.php to check against. A native Bengali-speaking water/fire-protection engineer should confirm this is the term actually used in design reports before it becomes the incumbent for future sprints.
readings: অগ্নিনির্বাপণ প্রবাহ ('fire-suppression flow', a compound built from ordinary words) (chosen)
A transliteration such as 'ফায়ার ফ্লো', which is common for borrowed engineering terms but was not chosen here since a Bengali compound reads more like a professional term of art
entries.resolution: The write-back this sprint owed. 'fire flow', 'available fire flow' and 'static pressure (fire flow)' all carried empty translations maps, so every language coined its own. The four anchor languages are now recorded in glossary.json from this sprint's own output, and the entry names the languages that flagged their coinage as unverified against their own fire code, which is the list a native reviewer should read first.

entries.complaint: The glossary's preferred_translation for 'emitter' is 'ড্রিপার' (literally 'dripper'), but the pre-existing, already-shipped key lpn_settings_emitter_exponent (not in this sprint's key list, so I could not change it) already uses the transliteration 'এমিটার' for the same concept. Following CLAUDE.md's rule to keep sibling keys parallel and consistent with what is already established in the file, I used 'এমিটার' in the new tip text rather than the glossary's 'ড্রিপার', so the two now disagree with the glossary but agree with each other.
readings: এমিটার (transliteration, matches the incumbent lpn_settings_emitter_exponent label already shipped) (chosen)
ড্রিপার (the glossary's preferred_translation), which would make this new string inconsistent with the existing label right next to it in the same Settings panel
entries.resolution: The agents were right and the glossary was wrong. entries.complaint: The English uses an English-only pluralization marker: '{n} node(s)'. Ukrainian numeral agreement has three forms (1 вузол, 2-4 вузли, 5+ вузлів) that an '(s)'-style marker cannot represent, and {n} is a runtime placeholder so the correct grammatical form cannot be chosen at translation time. I wrote '{n} вузла(ів)' as an approximate parallel to the English shorthand, but this is not real Ukrainian grammar, just a visual compromise.
readings: Keep the '(marker)' shorthand as an acceptable compromise, consistent across languages with numeral agreement
This string needs a genuinely different structure per language (e.g. dropping the noun entirely: 'for {n}?') rather than asking each translator to invent an ad hoc plural marker
entries.resolution: A genuine limit of '{n} node(s)' against languages with three-way numeral agreement, and not fixable by rewording the English alone. The agent's simplified-plural rendering is the accepted handling here; a real fix is plural-form support, which is a feature and not a string.
